utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, may we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution appearing with Mr. Turone, Mr. Cowles and Mr. Huber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Edina Residovic representing Mr. Zejnil Delic who is defended by my colleague, co-counsel Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan of Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Zeljko Olujic, Defence counsel of Croatia. I represent Zdravko Mucic, together with me he is represented by Mr. Tomislav Kuzmanovic all the way from the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Salih Karabdic lawyer from Sarajevo representing Mr. Hazim Delic together with Thomas Moran, a lawyer of Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Cynthia McMurrey, and along with Nancy Boler and Calvin Saunders we represent Esad Landzo. Mrs. Boler will be absent from the courtroom this morning. She has business to attend to outside. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mrs. McMurrey, we have your client for cross-examination, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which of you choose to have the cross-examination? Mrs. Residovic, I thought you were in charge; how did you organise your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I already stated that the Defence of Mr. Delic has no questions for this witness. The cross-examination will continue as in the indictment, starting with the Defence representing Mr. Mucic, followed by the Defence representing Mr. Delic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. Mr. Olujic, you may start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you are you still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Landzo. We will talk about certain matters. There is no need for me to introduce myself to you, you know very well that I represent Mr. Mucic. Everything that applied to the other witnesses when using our language, of course, also applies to this conversation of ours this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, when describing your physical and mental health since your childhood, do you think that you were physically less developed than the others in your generation?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, were you afraid of your peers?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Depends on who you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you allow others to beat you up at school?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, I had no problems throughout my school years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, we're having a technical problem. I hate to break into this, but we're not getting the transcript on the screen, and I don't know whether I'm pushing the wrong button or -- it's off and it won't go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you still have the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, the light that says off is lit and none of the other, or the one that's transcript, apparently that switch is broken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly get in touch with the technicians and they will come and see what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, apparently it can't be immediately fixed. I guess we'll have to live without it. I'm sorry for stopping the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it's only one, I don't know how we can adjust by moving a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The apparent problem seems to be that the switch itself is not working. And it's going to take some time to fix that, so we'll just have to live without it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for tolerating the inadequacies, we will look at it. You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honours, until this technical problem is offset Mr. Moran, if he wants to, can take my seat and follow the transcripts on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Karabdic will sit down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, we still have a minor technical detail to take care of. I apologise, Your Honours. We had to take care of these technical affairs so that my colleague, Mr. Salih Karabdic and myself can follow through the headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, in the course of the direct, you mentioned that you changed your former Defence counsel, my colleague, Mr. Bracinovic. Do you think that he was not defending you well?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, not the best defence and not the worst defence, either. He has not satisfied my requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, Mr. Landzo, in the course of the examination-in-chief, you also changed a second colleague of mine, Mr. Ackerman; do you think that he was defending you poorly, too?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I asked from him to let me make certain confessions, but he didn't allow me to do that. I thought that to a certain degree he should have followed my desires. I didn't want this trial to go on for such a long period of time. I wanted to shorten it, but he was against it for an unknown reason, and then simply he would not come to me to allow me to tell him the facts. He was not familiar with the facts. Maybe he was a good Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But if I said that he was not defending you well, would I be right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, that would be my general conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, when you sat into the witness bench, you said that you are doing this because other witnesses have not turned up; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Excuse me could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you sat on the witness bench, you said that you decided to appear here because the other witnesses, you wanted to speak on your behalf here in the Court; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I have been planning this for a longer period of time, but I also expected that the other guards from the Celebici camp would come to tell the truth. But since somebody or something prevented them from doing it, I was compelled to. And I also wanted to come here to sit at this bench and tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Landzo, what is something or someone who prevented them from coming here? Do you think this is a case of conspiracy against you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I can just tell you my opinion. I can't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But if I said that this is maybe a case of conspiracy because the witnesses did not turn up because as you say somebody or something prevented them from coming, would that be a conspiracy,?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I can tell you my opinion, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Could you answer me, please?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: The witnesses that were supposed to come here to testify are all fact witnesses, i.e. people who were in the Celebici camp who knew who was the commander and knew what was going on. It seems to me that somebody was against this line of thought, and that's why they didn't appear, I think. That's my opinion. But I will not go beyond this whole story. I think it's better for me to finish with this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So, this is a case of conspiracy, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: So it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Landzo, when describing your diseases, such as asthma, bronchitis and others, you said you were sick; do you often feel sick?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, that depends. Sometimes when the weather changes, sometimes I do, sometimes I don't. When I'm involved in certain physical activities. But that's only during the night when I try to go to bed, to sleep, then I have to put a bigger pillow under my head so that I can use the asthma devices, the pumps which help me to go asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Landzo, as an adult person, do you allow others to give you orders?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you say not now, tell me when did you allow others to give you orders?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Until some two years ago, perhaps. Yes, to tell me what to do. Until I have sufficiently stabilised my personality to be able to assume the responsibility for myself, instead of others doing this on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you think about yourself that you are a fighter for justice?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: A simple man living on this planet, I was a simple soldier who thought that it was his duty to defend the country, whether I am a warrior of justice or not, that's not up to me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I'm satisfied with your answer, thank you. Tell me, Mr. Landzo, you said that they called you by the nickname Zenga, when was the first time they used this nickname when addressing you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Somewhere at the end or beginning of 1992, the beginning of 1992, somewhere in February. I'm not sure, because this is the period upon my return, together with Cipeta from Herzegovina, that was perhaps in the following few weeks that, jovial and jokingly he started addressing me with the nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you were in Croatia, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: My assumption was that that was either western Herzegovina or Dalmatia, I really wasn't sure where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: We will talk about this at a later point in time. I have another question for you. Do you know where this abbreviation Zenga comes from?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: From where does it come?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: From Zbor Narodne Garde the legal military units in Croatia that resisted the then JNA forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Zbor Narodne Garde was founded?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know that they existed, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: If I said that Zbor Narodne Garde, at that time, when you were allegedly called Zenga had not existed, that is that this military unit was established through a decree of the Croatian headquarters in the summer of 1992; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I told you I don't know when they were founded. I just told you when they started using the nickname when addressing me. I don't know when this was founded. I also know that many Muslims from Bosnia were members of the military, of the internal affairs police and the Zenga units. You know, it's a lengthy procedure at war time to pass a law, so I don't know when they were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: At any rate, they did not exist at the time -- well, very well. Mr. Landzo, you said in the course of the examination-in-chief where my esteemed colleague was putting questions to you, you said that the HOS units were fighting around Zadar; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: My assumption was that it was somewhere in the direction of Knin I don't know exactly where they were fighting. I just related to you my assumption, my thought. I was not a military person so I was not able to investigate maps to know where exactly they were heading, so it was just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of units this could have been?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: What do you mean which?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What units, what were they called, these units?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't understand your question. Could you elaborate?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You said it was somewhere around Knin or Zadar that the HOS units were fighting; do you know what was the name of these units?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I'm quite happy if you say I don't know.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, they all called them HOS Croatian defence units or armed units, I don't know exactly what was the name of the individual units, I really don't know. Each unit had its own name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But you, yourself, say that you're just assuming, so you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I just know where I was, that there were people wearing black uniforms that, on their sleeves they had the round insignia with HOS and they also had the flag of the internal affairs units, what was the name of these units, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of an officer in this unit?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, you said that you stayed in a camp in the Republic of Croatia, you stated this in the course of the examination-in-chief, was this a camp training military units, or was this a detainee camp?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: You didn't understand me well, I didn't say this was in Croatia, I know that where I was, the houses looked like the houses that you usually find in Western Herzegovina and Dalmatia; whether this was Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina, I didn't know, I didn't have a map, I didn't know the name of the village, I didn't know the name of the town to be able to know exactly where I was, so this was not in Croatia, according to me, maybe it could have been in Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But you were able to identify this only on the basis of the stone made houses; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, because in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina this sort of houses are usually not found. This is typical of that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is Herzegovina and the part of Croatia which is Dalmatia, where they usually build houses in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: If I now enumerated to you five regions, provinces, where identical houses can be found, namely houses made of stone, would you agree that you could have at that time been at any part, any province, any region of either Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Could you enumerate them?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: These, this could be in western Herzegovina, it could be in Leca, it could be in Imotski, it could be Knin it could be in Istria, these are all stone made houses that you find there. The terrain is also shaped in a similar manner.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: You are right, but in Knin, you know it well, we couldn't go to Knin, when I use the term Dalmatia, I'm referring to the area from Dubrovnik to Rijeka when I say Western Herzegovina I'm referring to the territory which was under the control of the legal authorities, so I couldn't go to Nevesinje an or Trebinje in Eastern Herzegovina because there were Serbs there, so that was my assumption, we were heading from Konjic to Neretva, we turned to tarmac so it must have been a road from Herzegovina towards Dalmatia, it couldn't have been in Eastern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In any case, you do not know, either the place or the city in proximity of that camp?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I believe I have heard that close to that village there was one of the state roads leading to Split, but I really couldn't tell you whether that was in Croatia or in Bosnia. But as I concluded on the basis of the buildings, the configuration of the land, this is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: That was a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you come among other people?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Do you mean the inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can you name the people, the inhabitants, their names, give us their names with whom you contacted?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I believe that we spent the first night, his name, first name, was Jure, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And his wife's name?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Mara or Marija, something like that, I am not sure. And later on we would come and visit him and if they left us out of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, but I believe it was some 20 to 25 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You say that even today in Konjic, people know you by this nickname of Zenga, did you oppose that, were you against this nickname?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Even if I opposed it, I couldn't make them shut up or force them not to call me by that nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you said that you've spent some 25 days in the camp and that you also went out of the camp. How is it possible that you really don't know where the camp was? You know the name of the man where you spent the night, you know the name of his wife and you don't know which geographical location you were.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I can describe in which geographical area I was located and then you can conclude for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, I said I could enumerate five areas, five regions, which would be of the identical configuration. I only wanted an answer from you. How come that you spent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Don't you think you've made sufficient emphasis on that? You can move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, while staying in the camp, who was your first superior? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I can enumerate the names, but I am not sure. Some were called by their nicknames, so I cannot tell you exactly with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So if I assert that if I were to say that you cannot name the man who was your first superior, you couldn't state his name and surname, am I right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: That was not an organisation. In the morning, anybody would come in and wake us up, tell us to rise and would take us out to a shooting range. On the first day somebody came, the next day somebody else, the third day, the third day. If I were to see these people today, I would recognise them and I'd maybe know the nicknames by which they went, but I am not a computer mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I am satisfied. Mr. Landzo, do you know who was the first superior of the superior? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, I can assume --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, I want you to say only what you know.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What rank did the commander have?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: They called him Captain, but I saw no insignia, no ranks on his uniform. These were not regular formations as was the case with the JNA on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Are you sure he was called Captain?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes. That is what Jure told us. He told us to go to the Captain. I don't know whether that was just an expression he used or if he really had that rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: If I were to assert that in the Zbor Narodne Garde, nobody could be called a Captain, would I be right in that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I didn't say I was in that, in the ZNG. I said I was in a village where the HOS unit was stationed and I didn't mention Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: If I were to state that among the HOS units nobody would turn to his commander with the rank of Captain, would I be right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I heard that in Bosnia and in Herzegovina, I heard that some new ranks were introduced and Croatian terms were used for the ranks, but I am telling you what that man told me. I am not saying this is the truth. But that is what the man told us; to go to the Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the precise date when you came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I really cannot tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the month?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Approximately, if you want me to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, only if you remember.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, I can tell you approximately because the weather, it was warm, the period of warm weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Whom do you remember among your peers with whom you stayed in the camp 25 days? Can you remember these names and surnames and enumerate them?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Two or three names I remember. There was a group. They told me that they came from Central Bosnia. One's name was Osman, a Muslim. And the second one was Dragan and a third one Goran. These are the names that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can you remember any surnames?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, because we called each other by our first names. At present, I remember the surnames of some friends of mine with whom I spent ten or fifteen years, and not people with whom I spent 20 or 25 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How were the orders issued?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I told you it wasn't organised. They would just tell us, somebody would come and say, get ready, get your clothing ready, get your arms, weapons ready. And then they would order us to begin shooting. They would set a target, a bottle or a draw a circle on a piece of paper. It wasn't an organised camp. And that was my conclusion. And if somebody came, they would take him in, so that people would have their training. So there were no guard points. There was nothing like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You said in the examination-in-chief that heads were severed in that camp, is that true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: The name, names and surnames of those who perpetrated that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that. I can give you the nickname, one nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, I am satisfied with this. Do you know the names and surnames of the killed?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, we were told they were Serbs. They could have been Croats or Muslims, but we were told they were Serbs. But, of course, you cannot tell by their looks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, in what capacity did you come to Celebici? As a soldier or as a guard?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I was told to go there as a guard in the garrison where the young soldiers would be trained, where I would be a guard for a shorter period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So, I would be right in saying that you haven't come to Celebici as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: We were -- I came as a soldier, but in Celebici, I was given the task of being a guard. I could have been appointed as the commander. But I came as a soldier, but there I was given the duty of guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You already had military experience at the time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, I knew how to work with weapons, how to use weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Mr. Zdravko Mucic had no military experience?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: How should I know? Probably he served in the JNA, but on the basis of his age, I would expect that, but what really he did...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But it is true that he was neither a member of HVO, the units of the Ministry of Interior, the reserve units, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know that. I never saw any insignia on his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to ask you, did he have any military rank?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, at least not anything visible on the uniform. That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That is how we recognise the ranks, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, he didn't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, you have mentioned that you acted according to the rules of the service and that when you came to Celebici, you were told not to think and not to ask questions, but to execute orders, is that true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, can you tell us any rules or law by which this guard service operated?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I want to make it clear. We did not have written orders. We had orally stated orders to which we had to abide.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So there were no written rules for your service?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I have not seen them, nor has anybody ever shown them to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In Celebici, did soldiers come also from other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, two or three came from Modrica, that's Northern Bosnia and then refugees from Eastern Herzegovina, Nevesinje, I think they were guards later on. And then I believe two or three from Gacko, Eastern Herzegovina. But they stayed only a short period of time while I was there. But later on I heard that they would stay a bit longer in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, in Celebici, you also had an infirmary, is that true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In view of your many diseases, did you ever go to them for medical check-ups? You've said you've had frequent illnesses, what do you mean by that? You said you are frequently ill, but you have many diseases.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I only have asthma and it's a lifelong disease, which I have been having. But I asked for help in the Konjic Hospital. I had to, for example, receive an injection in the vein. The doctors in Celebici didn't have these injections, these drugs, and they couldn't help me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So I was right in saying that you were not asking for medical assistance in the Celebici infirmary?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: On a few occasions I did take sleeping pills. They gave them to me. I felt much more relaxed later on. Because during the night after a shift it's difficult to go to sleep, particularly if one had three or four shifts a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, during the examination-in-chief you stated that on the basis of orders you acted where detainees were beaten, but not beaten on the head. In order to avoid any bruises on the head they were the lower part of the body?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, if the order was to kill somebody, you had to do it by beating; namely, you were not allowed to kill somebody with firearms, but you had to beat him, but without injuring the head. Don't ask me why, I just did what I was ordered to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And who issued the order, this type of beating which would be invisible?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Either Mucic or Delic, but I am not sure. But probably it was Delic. It's more probable that it would be Delic, but I am not sure. But I am sure that it was somebody from the camp administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, do you know what was the rule of your guards that stated that guards are allowed to beat up the detainees?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know. I never served in the JNA to know the rules. I just followed the rules I was told to obey. Whether these were the rules of the guard service or anyone else, I don't know. I wasn't in a position to decide or to tell anybody about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that in Celebici the JNA rules concerning beatings and guard duty applied?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know what were the rules that were applied. Could have been those of the former JNA. Could have been somebody's personal rules, I don't know. I know that I, myself, and all the other guards would abide by the rules. We had to do it. Who adopted them? Who these rules were invented by before the war or during the war, I don't know. We were just told that we simply have no right to make up these rules, but rather, to abide by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know who were the guards who, together with you, would beat up the detainees?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: In most cases, I could tell you. I can just tell you that there was somebody, Ibro or Olujic, something like that. I don't know the other guards' names, but the other guards who were from Konjic, who came together with me, I can give you their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When they would come and say that there was no such order to beat up people so that bruises could not be detected, would they be right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, I would very much like them to come. I asked them to come, but they refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, you say that when you received these orders, you received them orally, if I understand you well, or rather, that they were never given to you in writing; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: All orders I personally received were oral. When somebody had to be killed, the person's name would be put down on to a piece of paper, but I have never received any order in writing. I was just told in a very inhumane manner, when somebody says, "I want to see this person go with his feet forward in the morning through the gate, the camp," then obviously, this is not something normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you were receiving these orders, was any other guard present?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I can't remember, but it's possible. You know, I was not alone there in the camp. There were other guards, but then when I was summoned to the office, then I was alone because not everybody could just go into the office, only when you were summoned were you allowed to go into the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can you give me the first name and family name of such guards?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I can give you the names of some of these guards. I cannot tell you who of the guards was present when I was given a specific order. I know that there were guards moving around, either outside the headquarters building or in the kitchen. There was always a guard around.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you said that you would beat people, hit people, do you think that that was right and honest on your part?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: If you ask me what is my opinion now then I will give it to you. Now I know, now I understand that this was not right. It was enough for them to be detained. But, at that time, I thought and I acted in the belief that I have to follow orders because I was really not allowed to think a lot because, as I said before, they had told us, you are not here to think, but to execute orders. So I would never really go to the person who issued an order to me and say, sir, I don't know think this is right. I was not allowed to do that, I had to do what I was told. And now, I think that this was very wrong because it was enough for these people to be detained, let alone afflict on them things that have been inflicted on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In the direct, concerning Counts 11 and 12 of the charges, here we are referring to Mr. Slavko Susic that was supposed to be put into Hangar No. 9. You said that you hit him twice at the entrance gate to Hangar No. 9; is this true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Tunnel No. 9, I hit him twice, but other guards hit him more often. I was not standing in a position from which I could really hit him hard, but there were other guards standing next to me. I did hit him twice, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In the direct you did not mention that you were ordered to beat him; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: If I got the order to hit him, I would have hit him more often. It was actually just pushing, it wasn't really hitting him. Because when the others started hitting him, I was told to take him to the hangar and not to hit him. So I was supposed to take him there. If I had been given the order to hit him, then it would have been a different story. I was just doing what I was told to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But that's not what I asked you, Mr. Landzo. I said the following: In the direct you said that the order was to take Mr. Susic to Hangar 9. And in the course of the direct, you also said that you hit him twice at the entrance gate to Hangar No. 9. However, when answering in the course of the direct, you never said that you were ordered to hit him. My question is just answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, I was not given the order, nobody asked me, had asked me whether I was given this order. I don't know how you can understand it, but these were really not any serious hits that could injure him. I couldn't get directly to him because there were three, four guards standing in front of him. I couldn't just grab him and take him to the hangar. I had to push him because I couldn't grab his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: As far as Counts 24 and 26 go, concerning torture of Spasoje Miljevic, in the direct, yesterday, you said you hit him at least once because he took the food away from the rest of the detainees. In the course of the examination-in-chief, you never said that you were ordered to hit him.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I slapped him, maybe I was not precise. It was a slap on the face and not a hit. Because how can you explain to an old man in front of you, crying, who a night before was hit in his head and the person who took away food from him standing next to him, how can you explain to him that the guy who took away the food from the older man was right. So I slapped Mr. Miljevic to show older detainee that the same law applies to old. But I didn't hit him, I just slapped him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you think that slapping is not beating up?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: One slap on the face? I wouldn't say that. I mean, it was done simply to comply with the old man's insistence on justice be done. Imagine what would have happened if I reported Miljevic, if this happened, then I guess Miljevic would never have been able to come here and testify. It all finished and ended with a single slap. And, in a way, I wanted to satisfy the old man's desire to bring peace to the hangar because it would have been, perhaps, easier to me to go to the headquarters and report Miljevic taking food away. Had I done this, Miljevic, would never be able, I guess, to come here and testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Have you reported the case?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Not me personally. I thought that this was the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, Mr. Landzo, what was the beginning and the end of your working day in Celebici? When you started and when you finished your duty.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: That depends on whether I was on duty or not. For example, sometimes I had to be on duty from 4.00 a.m. to 8. Sometimes from 8.00 to noon. Sometimes from noon to 6. I can't really give you a specific answer. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in the direct, concerning counts 36 and 37 of the indictment, concerning Nedjko (phoen) Draganic you said that Draganic was tied up and beaten up, he couldn't get up and the guard told you to lift him up and that he couldn't get up himself. Furthermore, you said that you hit him without having received an order to do so; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I didn't say that he was tied up. I just know that he had a cord on his left hand. I didn't see him tied up, I just saw a cord, a rope on his left hand. I got to him, slightly kicked him with my foot to make him get up. I did it three times. Then he couldn't get up, so I sort of pushed him up, but I didn't really hit him. I just helped him to get up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In the direct, you also stated that the people who would come to visit the detainees, that they could not see them at fence because that was not allowed, but that you gave the permission to Mr. Miljevic to see his mother who arrived there; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Did I say yesterday that I personally gave him the permission?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I was on the mound on my guard post when this old woman came to the fence. She was talking to Dedic Osman. And Dedic Osman asked me what are you doing? I told him that the woman was crying, that she didn't know whether he was alive or dead. And she said, imagine you were in his place, imagine your mother came here. And we decided, not me, but the two of us, we were talking to each other and we thought we would be allowed to take him for a few seconds to the entrance gate to let the mother see him. And Dedic Osman was standing along the fence to see whether anybody was coming or not, because that was not allowed. We did this in the sense of sympathy, we are not robots, our heart is not made of stone. There was this woman here who started crying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But you said that you always followed the orders. You even used the phrase "It was not up to us to think but to execute orders"?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Maybe this is what I'm guilty of.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So, can we say that you deviated from orders while you were staying in the Celebici camp from June to the end of July, as you say?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, there were these small details for which you didn't have to receive an order. For example, if a detainee wanted to go to the latrine, I didn't have to run to headquarters and ask for an order every time, to ask either the deputy, the warden or the commander. I could decide on my own. I would not let Miljevic to the fence. I just let him come as far as the entrance gate so that his mother could see him. There were these minor deviations, not only on my part, but on the part of the other guards. This is life, you can't be perfect. Everybody has sympathies, has feelings. No matter how far I tried to be a perfect soldier, I have feelings, I have a heart, and sometimes it would happen that these feelings would get the best of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were you proud of everything you had done at Celebici at that time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Proud?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I thought that was my duty. I was given an order, I had to execute. Whether I was proud, no. I was not (sic) proud to wear the uniform and the rifle, because I know that when you have a rifle you can kill. I felt safer, safer as far as my family, because I thought I could defend my family, but I certainly didn't feel proud.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Landzo, thank you, Your Honours, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will take us some time to get organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you have some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If I might bring a mistake in to the Court's attention. I believe the answer Mr. Landzo said when he was asked if he was proud to wear a uniform, he said he was proud to wear the uniform, and in the transcript it said he was not proud. So I hope that that can be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court, I think we're organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You've heard me talking to witnesses a whole lot of times, so you know I'm going to ask you to listen to the question, answer the question out loud and answer the question I ask. Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In fact, you've heard all the testimony here, haven't you? Essentially every word of it, you may have missed a couple of days because, for one reason or another, but you heard basically every word of testimony in this trial; haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, I was present and I did hear. But sometimes I was concentrated and listened to it in a concentrated fashion, but occasionally I wasn't, and I didn't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Are the transcripts on your computer, that little laptop you bring here?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but I cannot use it in the same fashion as you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But you have access to all of the transcripts. That's the question I've asked.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You don't like me very much, do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I can make it relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Don't make your questioning personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: A couple of weeks ago when we were upstairs and your witness, the psychiatric witnesses were testifying, you made a threat to me, didn't you, through your lawyer, about my cross-examination? Now was that a threat of getting on the witness stand to trash my client, or was that a threat of physical violence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. If he is saying there was a threat made, I would like to know what he is alleging because I'm not aware of any threat that was made through his lawyer to Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It was carried to me while we standing in the little alcove near that elevators where we went up and down at lunch one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm going to object, because I don't know what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, kindly go to the real issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You were here when Dr. Gripon testified yesterday, weren't you, Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And you heard his testimony. It was probably pretty hard for you to listen to, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear him, but it wasn't hard. He does, did his job, you're doing your job, and I'm also here to say what I believe should be said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And you heard Dr. Gripon testify that people with antisocial personality disorder, like you, will --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to him harassing the witness. When he says "like you", if he has a question about antisocial, can he phrase it not intimidating the witness like he's trying to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly put your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: As I said, you heard Dr. Gripon testify, one, that you have antisocial personality disorder, and two, that people with antisocial personality disorder will lie to accomplish their goals. You heard that; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Often, he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask the question with that qualification.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That they will often lie to achieve their goals. You heard that didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear, but let me answer to that. I have come here to tell the truth, but if this truth does not meet the needs of your client or anybody else, that doesn't mean that I lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, that's what we're here for, is the truth. Let's talk about some truth. Yesterday on your direct you testified about an incident where you had an apartment, and you had gotten some vacant apartment you moved into and changed the locks, and these owners apparently were back in there and you went in and fired a, fired into the ceiling; do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Is that the same incident that you told Dr. Lagazzi about, the first time you talked to him, when you said you threw a hand grenade into an apartment where there were some women? Or was that a different episode?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I never, and to anybody did I ever state that I threw a hand grenade, because nobody would survive, they would be dead. I said to him and others that I shot three or four times from the rifle, three or four times in the ceiling. If I threw a hand grenade I wouldn't be alive today, and neither would anybody else be. I know what happened, and I know what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So, if Dr. Lagazzi in his report dated 15 November, 1996, which is in evidence as D61/4 said, quote, "He also remembered that he was promised a house to move into, but when he arrived at the door drunk he found four girls who had found shelter inside. He was angry, so he threw a hand grenade in the entrance and fired a burst of fire from the machine gun, lightly injuring the girls who escaped into an another part of the apartment". Dr. Lagazzi, if he said you said that, he would be wrong; wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, you would have to ask the translator, and not Dr. Lagazzi or me. I know what I said and I know Dr. Lagazzi will tell you what he understood. So probably you would have to ask the person who was translating on that occasion. Because I'm sure that he wrote in the report what was being translated, and I know what I've said on the occasion, so you have to ask the person who was translating at the time. I cannot say whether Dr. Lagazzi is right or wrong. I know what I stated, and I stand firm on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So, either Dr. Lagazzi or --?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think he answered that. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Is that the same incident, the incident you discussed yesterday, is that the same incident where there was a young man in a flat, in a flat occupied by a young man? That's the one you were talking about; right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that there were two incidents of violence after you left Celebici, and the apartment incident was one of them. And you said there was another one with your brother. We had a break, coffee break, and nobody ever followed it up, and I'm going to ask you this: Is that incident with your brother, is that the one that, where you went into the bar and had the drinks and when the bill came, rather than pay the bill you fired up into the ceiling? Is it that the other incident of violence you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I never said that I was firing in the ceiling because the bill arrived. It's true that there was this incident with my brother, but that I'd be shooting in a restaurant because of the bill? I don't remember of saying that, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Why were you shooting in the restaurant, then, if it wasn't over the bill? Just to do it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Can you, could you maybe read it to me out? Maybe I said it, but I cannot remember. Could you read it out to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident, do you remember telling Dr. Gripon, who I think is still sitting out there, about an incident when you went into a bar with some other soldiers after you left Celebici, and drinking, and then when you left, firing into the ceiling? Do you remember telling Dr. Gripon about that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I cannot remember. Maybe I said it, but if you remind me, if you read it out to me. I had a number of meetings with Dr. Gripon, we talked on many subjects. We spoke about these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did the incident occur, Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Possibly. I cannot remember. I know that there was that incident in the apartment and with my brother, the incident with my brother, but about this one, I do not remember. If you can tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What was the incident with your brother? I was asking if that was the incident with your brother.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, no, no it's not that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What was the incident with your brother, then, the incident of violence? Tell the Judges what it was.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I found this apartment for myself, and I accepted my brother and some three or four friends from the military police to live with me. However, they sold all of the furniture from the building. Later on the police came and they gave me a decision that I should move out of that apartment. Then I moved back to my father's place, and I came home from my duty as, in military policeman, I came very tired. And let me say that while I was still living in that apartment, my brother would always bring in the evening friends, there was a lot of music and they were having fun, I never could rest. And when I returned back home to my father's place, once I came home I wanted to rest and go to sleep. This brother came home with his friends, I asked him then to not come at the time, that he should come a bit later, but he pushed me. And in my reaction it wasn't with intention, it was a matter of seconds, I shot a few shots in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So, this is a second incident in an apartment?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Who ordered you to fire those shots the second time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Who ordered you to fire the shots the first time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Nobody. I felt threatened. I felt that my life was threatened. That is the period when I was working in the military police, and the first case, when I came to the apartment, there were three young men in uniform with weapons. And I felt threatened, and these were warning shots. I didn't want to injure them. And obviously that is why I also shot in the ceiling, in order not to injure them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Now, those were the only two incidents of violence after you left Celebici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: After leaving Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Well, how about that incident you talked to Dr. Lagazzi about, where you and some of your co-fighters got drunk and hung a woman by her heels from the top of a tall building because she refused to go with you? Would you consider that to be an act of violence?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I held her? I know that that happened. I was present at that occasion, but I couldn't hold her. I was present in that group, but I wasn't holding her by the feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: We may have had a translation problem and I don't speak enough Bosnian to know. But the word you, Y-O-U in English can be singular and plural, and if it was translated singular it was meant to be plural, it was meant to be you as the group of fighters. So, I didn't say you personally held her. You being you and your co-fighters. That was not -- ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why do you use the word co-fighters? Say companions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I'm using the word co-fighters because that's the word Dr. Lagazzi used in his report on page 17 of exhibit D61/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You wouldn't consider that to be an incident of violence, then?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but I didn't take part in it. As you, in order to understand the situation, I must explain to you what people, type of people were involved, and then what state they were in, in order to make you understand the entire situation. It's difficult for someone who comes from a normal situation to understand the situation we had in our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Because at the time a pebble on the road, was more valuable than human life.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Who was it that ordered you in that incident, with the girl hanging by her feet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said he did not do it himself, so the question of somebody ordering him does not arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How about an incident where some girl looked you up and promised that if you killed her father they, actually I think the phrase Dr. Lagazzi used is "promised herself and her sister to him," him being you, if he, you, killed their father, who was violent and abusive, and that when you found him in a drunken state, you only injured him. Would you consider that to be an act of violence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did he remember that incident you're asking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that incident? Let's start off with that.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, I know that these two girls and their mother asked me to do that. However, when the shooting did take place there were ten who shot him. So, it's a question who shot him. That was from the railroad station, the Serbs were leaving. And from the battalion command we were told to shoot warning shots to all people who were moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So, when Dr. Lagazzi says in his report, the last part of the sentence being, "and so he found him in a drunken state but only injured him," Dr. Lagazzi, that must have been a mistranslation of some kind? Another mistranslation? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's a mistake, I know what I've said. I know when the man was injured. I later on visited him in the hospital. And it wasn't only I who was shooting, there were, we were all shooting. Nobody was allowed to move along that road, be it Serbs, Muslims or Bosnians, and nobody was allowed because many had been killed along that road. It's true there were drunken people on the front-line at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So that incident was just in the line of duty.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: You would have to ask them what I said. I didn't want to do it, because if I wanted to do it, I would do it in the city and not there. I've never had any intention to shoot him. We only had to carry out the order of stopping people from moving along that road. That was the situation. Many people were injured, there was shooting going on, also from the side of the HVO and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So that incident, Mr. Landzo, was in the line of duty as a soldier, right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was on the front-line at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident, sir, where you came across several of your co-fighters that had found a Serb who had gotten some cigarettes as a gift from a butcher and they were arguing among themselves over who was going to get the cigarettes? Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I can tell you what -- ?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object, he is misleading the witness. The incident that he's referring to occurred in Celebici, and he is talking post Celebici violence, so I would like them to give him a time frame, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me read you what Dr. Lagazzi says. And this is on page 18 of exhibit D61/4. I'll read it out, and if would you like I will have it brought over to you. Dr. Lagazzi says, quote, "As an example, he described an episode in which he was involved, some of his co-fighters had found a Serb who had received several packets of cigarettes as a gift from a rich butcher, and they argued among themselves, beating him in the meantime, in order to establish who should get those cigarettes. Esad tried to calm down the colleagues by dividing the cigarettes among them and then he walked away. He had later gone back on his own and started beating the man for no reason, though neither seriously injuring nor killing him." Okay, now start off, was that incident in Celebici or was it post Celebici, or do you not recall the incident?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I would be distributing cigarettes to my colleagues? I never did it, because I never smoked, and I can't recall having done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, so, either you forgot, or there is some other problem with Dr. Lagazzi's report, and you just don't recall the incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to him putting words in his mouth. If he lets him respond he will explain what the circumstances were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is cross-examination and I believe I'm allowed to ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will rise for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What she is saying is misleading, not leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Jan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will return at noon.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, both over the break we just had and the breaks yesterday, did you discuss your testimony with anybody?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I talked to my Defence lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: The question was, did you discuss your testimony with anybody? I didn't ask if you were --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, is he asking for a violation of attorney/client privileged information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, why don't you let him ask his questions. He merely asked a simple question. If he discussed it with anybody, he would say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he discussed it with his lawyer, that still is part of privileged information and confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, if he said so. That would be understood. Would you please leave him to conduct his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, the question was, did you discuss your testimony with anybody? That's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, with my lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much. You've now answered the question. Now, let's go on to something else. Mr. Landzo, again, just reminding you of Dr. Gripon's testimony about goals and things. What's your goal here in testifying?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: To feel once again like a human being. To tell you the truth, I came here to tell the truth because I want to be a human being. And if you are aiming at my release from the prison, this is not what I am after. I want to be punished for what I am guilty of. I don't want to be punished for what I am not guilty for. I am not afraid of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In fact, you expect to be sent to a prison in either in Western Europe or in the United States, preferably the United States; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to this line of questioning. It's totally to the guilt and innocence stage of this trial. Irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think it's goes to the mind set of this defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You ask him your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In fact, you want to serve any sentence you have in Western Europe or the United States, preferably the United States; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I am examining this possibility. If I have to be sentenced to prison, I would like to use this time for education. I would like it to be a country that will allow me to use my prison sentence to spend it to learn something for tomorrow so that when I am released to be able to live in the future. Whether this is Western Europe or the United States of America, that's of the least importance. I am just heading for a country that will allow me to do that if that's feasible. I want the best future possible. I don't want to be what I used to be, somebody without anything and nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: After your sentence is up, whenever that would be, you expect to continue to reside in the United States; right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: That's what I never said. I was thinking about this desire to live there because it's a big country. It has enormous opportunities. People who don't know me. I could start my life from afresh. The United States of America, or Canada, or those countries that are far away from Europe and, specifically, far away from Bosnia. Because I certainly don't want to go back to the old. If that is a sin, then I am a sinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You came up on this idea of moving to the United States and becoming a permanent resident all on your own?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me put a question mark at the end of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you're putting a question, that's a different thing, but he did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And did you come up with this idea of moving to the United States all on your own?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is not specifying the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Or Canada, all on your own?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I talked to my lawyer about the possibilities, what the possibilities are to spend my sentence in the United States of America, in Canada, in Sweden. So I was thinking along these lines. I would opt for the United States of America because there is an enormous opportunity for a better life there, but that's not to mean that I want to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Probably be good in a new society. I think you should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, very first thing, off the bat this morning, you were talking about Mr. Brackovic. This is just my notes and I may not be exactly correct, okay. And, if I am not, just stop me and correct me. But my notes said that; you didn't get the best Defence, it wasn't not the worse Defence and he had not satisfied your request. Now, you never said what the request was. Was the request that he pay you money? Is that the request you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am still going to object, this is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think given some of his statements yesterday, and that statement this morning, at least to that extent, I think he may have waived the attorney/client privilege. In fact, I recall, and I can find it if you give me a minute. I can recall standing up yesterday when he made some charges against Mr. Brackovic and suggesting that he may have been on some pretty thin ice as it applies to the privilege and Mr. Brackovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: His evidence was fairly clear. This relationship with Brackovic and why he fired him. It was very clear. But it included a portion of his enemies to his family. He said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the question that I had was that the request that Mr. Brackovic did not comply with that he was discussing this morning. Did he mention this morning. Right out, first thing. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two reasons, not just one. If you will recall my testimony of yesterday, I mentioned two reasons, not just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of the reasons, as I recall from your testimony yesterday, you noticed that Mr. Brackovic was having problems with Ms. McMurrey. That's on page 15110 of the transcript, lines 18 through 23. And the second thing you said was, that he wouldn't pay you money because he said it was unethical. Now, this morning you said; he was not the best Defence and not the worse Defence and he had not satisfied my request. And what I am asking is, is the request that he did not satisfy, that he refused to pay you money? That's a pretty simple question.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: That is not the only reason. I will give you the reasons from the very beginning. I asked him to let me tell the truth and he said, no, that's not in the interest of the country for truth to be told here if you want me to tell you the truth. I will not keep quiet because I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Right now I believe that Mr. Moran is maybe going to approach the breaching of the confidentiality with Mr. Brackovic and Mr. Landzo. I don't believe that the Court has ruled yet that that privilege has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that not part of his evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exact quote and it's page 15110, lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You were in court yesterday when this evidence was given. I am sure you knew about it. You knew when he gave the evidence. You approved of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just for the record on pages 15116 and 15117, starting at line 17, the record reflects that I stood up and said, "Excuse me, Your Honours, I think we're going, we may take the position at some future date that this defendant is in the process of waiving his attorney/client privilege with Mr. Brackovic. And we may be calling Mr. Brackovic as a witness. I think at this point the Court might want to, at least inform the witness, that he is on thin ice as to the attorney/client privilege." And the record reflects that the Presiding Judge, Judge Karibi-Whyte said, "That's correct. I think Mr. Brackovic is not represented here and accusations having been made against him, his family, his counsel so he needs to protect his interests in this regard." It's not something, Your Honour, that anybody should be surprised about today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think counsel was here when the allegation was made and if counsel did not even want allegation to be made, she should have rejected it from the beginning because it wasn't fair on Mr. Brackovic and I expect he should be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I am not sure, the attorney/client privilege varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. But in the jurisdictions that I am familiar with, the privilege is gone to the extent that a client accuses his lawyer of misconduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In fact, you don't talk about privilege when the witness himself volunteers these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The privilege, of course, belonging to Mr. Landzo, not to any of his lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Let's try it one more time, Mr. Landzo. The question was: This morning you said he has not satisfied my request. And the question I put to you was: Was that request that he turned down a refusal to pay you money? That requires a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said one of the considerations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He said there is not only that, there are others. He said at least. He was trying to name the things he had against his counsel. And he indicated, he started indicating it when, perhaps the examination came. So he might be in a position to state what are the other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, what are the other things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Those are the two requests?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: If I may, let me give you an explanation. Maybe something is not quite clear here. Yes, as far as financial help is concerned, I was not strongly on the stand to fire him because of that. Had Mr. Delic not given me this advice, telling me that his lawyer was helping his family at that time, my father was working for a salary of around 80 Deutschmarks per month. So what I tried to do is get some financial assistance from my lawyer. He would, however, come to me saying "I spent last night in the casino. I lost some money," and instead of being willing to help me, he would do that. So I was not firm on firing him until another person, almost on a daily basis while walking with him, advised me what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You talked about that financial assistance, okay, you brought it up, let's talk about it. That financial assistance was financial assistance, it was provided on behalf of the SDA party, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, that financial assistance was paid to your family also in amount of 200 Deutschmarks a month by the SDA to help your family until what? January of this year?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: But not regularly. You should ask why they were paying it. They weren't paying it because they like me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: The SDA party ask you to do anything wrong? Did you get a letter from Alija Izetbegovic saying do this or do that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Not directly, but through my lawyer. And this is why I decided to have no single lawyer from the territory of the former Yugoslavia, because here there are lots of things involved that I don't want to talk about because I don't have evidence to corroborate a statement. This is something else that I really don't want to go into.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Not all of them, but certain lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And we just wanted to -- okay, you don't have to go into it if you don't want to, I'll be gracious. Let's talk about some of your testimony from yesterday, okay. First thing I would like to talk about is the incident where you cut your hand. Remember that? Remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And you remember the incident, of course, because you testified about it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it, maybe not all the details, but I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And you grabbed that knife in anger because you blamed your father because you couldn't go to art school, right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, that's not true. At that moment, there was no mention made about the art school when this misunderstanding took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. When you grabbed it, you were angry, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Like any teenager in adolescence, everything bothers you unless it is just the way you think it should be. That's normal for all persons. Well, it's not normal to react in this way, but that was a time of my personality development, so even for trivial things, I would be really pissed off. Later on, I recognised that there was no genuine reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall testifying yesterday when you were asked -- excuse me, not yesterday, the day before yesterday -- about that incident? You said, "I don't know why I became quarrelling with my father, but that was in 1991, when I couldn't attend the art school. And after this impossibility of attending this school, I was to -- I blame everything, my father for everything. And then we quarrelled, the two of us.
