And simply, I became nervous and I grabbed something I found in a cupboard, a knife. I really don't know why I grabbed the knife. And I hit against this cupboard. And on that occasion, I slipped and cut four fingers." Do you remember testifying to that? I would be happy to show you the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: There are mistakes in the transcript. I didn't hit it once, more times. I did it once only. I blamed his father without good reason. But, at that time, I blamed everyone for not being able to go to art school. At that time, when something was wrong at school, when I couldn't get something, I would always blame my father. And whenever we would start a discussion, I would reproach him for not allowing me these things to do. So the topic of the misunderstanding at that time was not the art school. But I blamed my father for everything because I thought that he should have enabled me to do these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So when you centred that testimony on the art school, that was just you were centring on the art school and there were a lot of reasons you were mad at your father. Is that what you're saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, you seem to have misunderstood me. For all misunderstandings, since the time I left the art school, when my father couldn't finance my art school, everything that happened, together with the school, my future, I would blame my father. Now I know I had no reason, but at that time, I blamed him for not enabling me to finish what I wanted to finish. There didn't have to be tied only to the school, to the Konjic school. But this is how I blamed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, fine. By the way, when was that incident when you cut your hand, roughly, if you know the month and the year. It was 1991, we know that. What month was it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I think it was February. If I -- well, as far as I can recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And you had some surgery after that, right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: On the second day after the injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was your hand in a cast at all? Did Dr. Buturovic put your hand in a cast?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, upon the surgery, I think I had the cast on for about one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And, after the cast came off, he did some threading, put some threads on your hand or something so you could work with it? Do you remember testifying about that? Through the 4th and 5th finger, he pulled a thread through it, when was that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: He put me, the thread immediately upon surgery. It was here, through the skin he would insert the cord, the thread, and put it on to a rubber so it was elastic so I could do exercises because there was certain clearance between the hand itself and the cast, so as to be able to move the fingers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And all of that came off, when? In March 1991?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, I know that I had it for about a month, the cast, that I am sure of. And then the cast was removed and I graduated from the school. But, of course, I was out of school, I couldn't write. I couldn't attend classes. I couldn't do practical work. So, at the end of the year, I had to sit for the exams.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did the threads and everything come off when the cast came off, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And then you, because you couldn't go to school, you had to sit for all your exams at the end of secondary school, at the end of the year, end of the school year; right? Did I understand that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, no. Before the school was out, I had extra classes and I graduated on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When do you have graduation from secondary school in Konjic? I know in America we do it -- I can tell you exactly we did it in May 30th this year where I come from because I was there for my daughter's. When was yours? What day of the month, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether it was in April, May, June, July?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No. If you showed me a document, I would be able to confirm it, but otherwise I can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know that it was 1991, but the month I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That's -- okay. So you just have no idea?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Let's talk about something else and this may be a translation error, and, if it is, I think we need to point it out to everybody. The day before yesterday, you were talking about joining the TO, okay? And --

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And on page 15024 of the transcripts at lines 24 and 25 and then line 1 on the next page, you -- the transcript says, "And Miro told me to sign up to the TO, Territorial Defence, which had its headquarters in the Ministry of the Interior." And then a couple of pages later, on page 15026, lines 9 through 13, you talk about Miro insisting that you stay with him, you don't join the army. And he said you were too young, it wasn't the war for you. The war is for nobody, for no wise person. Which is right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Let me explain. May I explain it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Well, you can start off with telling us which is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel is not blaming you for what has been said, whether you know the two versions which are not consistent, which is a correct version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Is it a mistranslation the first --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They're both true. But, I forgot to explain the first version. Can I explain it now? Both of them are true. If I am allowed to explain it, then it will be clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Why don't you explain version one first and then go on to version two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The two have to be explained together. Let him do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, that is, I can't recall exactly what was the time. Cipeta and myself insisted from Miro on a daily basis, to send us to the Territorial Defence. He refused to comply. I think it was ten times a day that I asked him. He had a machine gun of his own, which he got from the Ministry of the Interior. He had it in his room, but we couldn't carry it around because we were not members of the Territorial Defence. We insisted on it. He had a friend of his with the Territorial Defence, who was head of a TD unit and he told me, go there and apply there. I went there, I found the person in question. This person told me, what are you guys going to do here? And he sent me back. When I came back home, Miro was laughing and he asked me, did they take you in? My conclusion was that he just wanted to help us, perhaps, he called them by phone and told them not to take us in. He just wanted to get rid of us because we really bothered him, ten, fifteen times a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, so Miro was only joking he when he told you to join the TO the first time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Not joking, he probably wanted to satisfy our desire, but it turned out the way it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And Miro forgot about that when he testified?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: If I remember, nobody asked him about it. If you had asked him, I'm sure he would have told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure he would have, too, sir. While we're thinking about Miro, Miro said that you were unloading 20-ton trucks. You recall that testimony, and lifting televisions and things. And your testimony, I'm looking for it now, but as I recall, if you want me to look for it, I'll find it, but as I recall what you said was, you mainly just shoved boxes and things, and if there were smaller trucks, and if you needed help someone would be hired, folks would be hired to do that; right? Do you remember saying something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, but I did the unloading, and of course there were a number of people there. The truck would come in front of the shop, one or two people would be on the truck, and that they would push the goods closer to the edge of the truck, the others would take, unload and take the goods to the warehouse, and the third group would then be putting it in the warehouse. And always when we were unloading bigger trucks, we would invite people whom we knew and who would be paid. We couldn't do it alone. Only in cases of smaller trucks, Cipeta and I would do it alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And Miro forgot about hiring all those people when he testified about you unloading 20-ton trucks. Or nobody ever asked him; right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: You should have asked him. I don't remember, recall anybody asking him. You, I remember what it was, but you can ask him. He was the one who paid these people. For example, Bubalo Esad, he helped me a number of times in unloading the truck. And Miro always paid these people who were helping us for the short time of unloading. He paid them. But you can check it out with Miro, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And it must have been tough unloading those trucks with your hand. Was it hard to unload things like the television sets that Miro talked about?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I was unloading everything that I was asked. I was on the truck always, and I then would unload half a metre, but I never carried the goods to the warehouse. But I helped in the warehouse in order to know where everything was when Miro would ask us where the goods were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So all you would do is pick it up off the back of the truck and set it on the ground, or the loading dock?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, you know, the small trucks were about a metre wide. I would step, let's say, make a metre or two step there and move the goods. That is why I was on the truck, because I couldn't carry these goods for a longer period of time, and longer routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And it was hard, I bet it was hard, too, both with your asthma and your hand when you carried that lumber to Miro's father's house. That was tough, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: These lumber, the lumber, that was really waste, these waste, these were small pieces, I don't know how to explain it to you. This was waste lumber. After the cutting and the mill, I could do that, it was easy. It's not that you had big chunks of wood. Miro's father used that for a furnace, for the boiler for his central heating.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thinking about your health, as I recall, one of the Dutch physicians, the pulmonary physician, testified that you have an allergy to dust; is that right? Let me rephrase, you're allergic to dust; right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, dust, feathers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And dust causes you to have an asthmatic reaction, have an asthma attack?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, problems, breathing problems, I have difficulty in breathing. It's not an attack where I can't move. I have problems, breathing problems, but in a day or two, if you don't prevent that, then a more serious stage occurs, sets on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Fine, let me go on to another subject, sir. You testified, as I recall, that when you were first assigned to the Celebici camp there was some kind of a guard position in, I think you called it, I don't want to say -- I call it a fox hole, okay? Some kind of a hole dug in the ground that was in front of hangar 6, but it's not on the model; do you recall testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And you had a machine gun there that was to both cover the front of hangar 6 and to prevent people from breaking into the camp to harm the inmates? Didn't you testify to that? I'm looking for it right now. I believe that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: It wasn't my machine gun. It was a machine gun that was located there, but it's not that I would have it there whenever I wanted. It was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand it was stationed with the guard post.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, and at the beginning two guards were sitting there. After that one was moved to this mound.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And in fact, one of the reasons it was moved to the mound was because you were stationed there in that guard point and didn't like being, you call it I think a ditch, I call it a fox hole, being full of water. You wanted something drier; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: That wasn't the reason. I was ordered to have this, hold this position in order to have better control over the entire facility. It was not wet only in the fox hole, it was wet also where I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So, when your lawyer asked you on page 15034 of the transcript at line 15 and 16, you said, "Now the dugout on top of the hill there, that was your idea to create that dugout, wasn't it?" And on line 17 the answer starts off, "Yes, when I was ordered to be in the guard post I was always sitting in the field, but you know if a car passed or some drunken soldiers passed by they would shoot at me. That's why I asked Mr. Delic if we should do something." So, was that just some kind, did I misunderstand, that it wasn't your idea to build that guard post on the top of the hill?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: My idea was to dig the fox hole. And it, of course, wasn't up to me to decide where the guard post was. There were also other guards there, and we had to sit in that field. And quite often it would happen that somebody was shooting from the village, the direction of the village, and there was a great danger that people would, a person would be hit. That is why I wanted, I thought that a shelter would be made, and Mr. Delic approved that, said that I could take and engage two or three people from hangar 6 and that we dig that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, fine. And they dug out a dugout, and they put a roof on it; didn't they, so you could sleep in it? Wasn't it covered?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In fact, show the judges on the model where it is, so we can all be sure what we're talking about. Just walk around and point to it.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Thank you very much, sir. And you slept in there because you were, because of your health problems. You moved a bed into that bunker; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, we didn't make, I made a bed there. And the reason why I slept there, namely when the shift would end, we couldn't find, often, a free bed to sleep, and we would sleep in the kitchen on the table. That, even that bed, it wasn't used just by me, but also by other guards, quite often so. And I didn't sleep always, every day there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, so if the transcript reflects on page 15035, beginning on line 6, you discussing the premises, and you couldn't find a bed and sometimes it was too hot and too cold. And then you, starting at line 8 you say "Often, due to my health problems, I couldn't shift constantly from cold to hot and vice versa, and that is why I set all of this up," this being the bunker. "And I could sleep there, I could be on duty there. This was a dugout made of two parts. The guard would be sitting and watching while I would be sleeping." There were other reasons besides your health, the hot and cold that you set up that bed and everything in the bunker; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: When I'm speaking of the hot and cold, I was speaking also, I was thinking of Building D. I slept there in the hall where it was very cold. I was sleeping near the lavatories. And the administration building, there was a lot of heat, and it was also a hot building in summer. So, that is why I linked this up, combined this. And that is why I made this makeshift bed. I didn't make it only for myself. Other guards were also using it. Neither the dugout nor this bunker, nor the bed. I slept on quite a number of occasions, but not only I.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And maybe you can help me with this, Mr. Landzo. Every bunker I've ever been in, every one of what we would call a field fortification is a pretty dusty thing. It's dirty. It's a hole dug in the dirt. If you're allergic to dust, wouldn't that affect your asthma if you were sleeping in there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: If you've listened carefully to the doctor, I was allergic to house dust. And we had wood planks on the floor, there wasn't really very much room. There was some dust, of course. And there was dust also before the hangar, in the hangar, and dust also here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, so you're just allergic to some kinds of dust. I understand now, sir.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: That is what the test has shown. Maybe I'm allergic to all types of dust, but if I remember correctly it's house dust, it's feathers, and a change of climatic condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Also, here in my cell I have problems when I dust my room, after that I have to use a spray.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, fine. And let me go on to a different subject, sir. One more thing before I leave the bunker, okay? And that bunker on the top of the hill, the one you just pointed to, there was a machine gun there; wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, later this machine gun was found in Bradina, it was brought to the camp, cleaned, and it was placed, located there where I was often on guard. There was a machine gun also at the entrance gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So, we have got that machine gun there, and let's set aside the one at the entrance gate, okay? We had that machine gun there, and then we had -- by the way, it had ammunition, didn't it? It could fire.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, I think some 30 bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And you had another machine gun that was in that ditch that's out in front of hangar 6 that, the ditch that was always full of water; or are those the same machine gun?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, there were two, and the water was in the fox hole only when it rained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But I was just discussing the fox hole with the water in it, the one directly in front of hangar 6. That had a machine gun that had ammunition, and the one on the top of the hill had a machine gun that had ammunition, and both of them could cover the area in front of the hangar 6; right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes. The, we, on the hill we wanted to cover the exterior perimeter of the camp. We had to -- in the beginning we had M-48 rifles with five bullets, after that automatic rifles with ten bullets; and with ten bullets, you could not defend if there were people who would be attacking with automatic rifles. At the time we didn't have in the camp any automatic rifles, that was the purpose of the machine guns there. And it wasn't my decision to place them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, I understand, sir. You were just a guard, and you didn't make those kinds of decisions. I understand that, and nobody is criticising you for that, sir. I just wanted to make sure I understood there were two machine guns covering the front of hangar 6. And there were.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, no. One controlled the entrance to the hangar, the other covered the exterior area in front of the camp, the village, in order to control the entrance. Because the one on the hill couldn't cover the entrance gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. And you were afraid that the prisoners were going to riot, right? And you were afraid because you only had two M-48 rifles, each guard had one M-48 rifle with ten rounds of ammunition and that's why you were worried that the Serbs might do something, might overwhelm you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, that was what we were told, to be always on guard. Also, when we communicate with the detainees, you know, I only arrived there at that time. I didn't know the people, I didn't know what was happening. That was the idea I had, that they were dangerous people, ready to do everything. And now what can I do with five bullets for a rifle and with 200 detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, fine. By the way, it must have been tough to work that bolt action rifle with your hand; wasn't it? Could you work it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: You said that you were in the army. As you know, you can cock it with two fingers. I mean, you were in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Actually, sir, the weapons I used in the army, to be quite frank with you, were not bolt action rifles. I have very little experience with bolt action rifles.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: It was like a hunting rifle, a carbine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, in fact, there is a picture around here some place if we really want to look at one. Let me jump on to another subject. Without going into any of the details, okay? Because I'm not going to ask you the details about it. And if your lawyer wants to do it on redirect, that's fine, but I'm just asking you in general, okay? Back in 1992 and '94, you gave some statements to the authorities in Bosnia about a crime you were accused of; right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the murder of Bubalo?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thinking about the Bubalo case. Without going into detail, you gave statements about that to the Bosnian authorities; right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: In 1992, it wasn't an official statement, but in 1994, an official statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And those statements were not truthful, were they?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you, I would have to look at them. There were some things which I said then which were not truth, the truth; but I would have to look at them in order to be able to tell what you is the truth and what is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That's what I was asking you, that those statements were not completely truthful, and you knew they were not truthful when you made them; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes. At the time of my detainment in Pasovici village there were statements that I made. You know, some were at midnight, you would be taken out of the cellar, they would give you a paper with a written statement and they would order you to sign. So, I would sign without checking on them. There were such statements, but there are also statements where I know what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the statements that you knew what you said you didn't tell the truth in; did you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: If you can show me the statement, then I will be able to answer you. Like this, I know there are things that I said that were true and there are things that I said that were not true. If you can show me the statement, then I can be more specific about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Actually, sir, I'm just asking about, I'm not asking about individual details. I'm just asking whether the statements were truthful. And here's why: Remember back on the 18th day of July, 1996, you were interviewed by a man named Bart D'Hooge and Mrs. McHenry, in the presence of your lawyer in the U.N. Detention Centre.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And they were talking to you about some statements that you made in 1994 to an investigating judge. Okay? And Mr. D'Hooge asked you on page 5 of the statement, "Did you sign any statements?" And you answered, "Yes". And then Mr. D'Hooge says, "When you were interviewed, did you tell the truth?" And you said, "no". And he responded, "You didn't tell the truth?" And you said "No." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Can you show this document to me? I cannot recall it. I cannot recall that part of the interview. I know that I was interviewed, that I made statements, but I don't know exactly what I said. I know that we had this interview. I know that the gentleman put questions, but I don't know exactly what I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Could we provide him a copy of his statement to the OTP? I've forgotten what the number is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 102.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, I could tell you, sir, that it's on page 5 of the English version. I have no idea where it would be in the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You don't have any problem with that being a correct transcription of the videotape of that conversation you had with Mrs. McHenry and Mr. D'Hooge; do you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I believe that this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: You know, as I said before, some statements are not true, some are true, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And the reason you gave in there for telling an untruth was because your lawyer in the Bosnian proceedings, whose name I don't remember -- what was his name, by the way?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Mr. Brackovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, the one in the Bosnian proceedings. You gave another name some place in your statement. Someone else represented you, you said in your statement to the OTP, at least.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Fejzagic Esad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That's right, and the reason you give in your statement for not telling the truth was he told you not to tell the truth; is that right? He recommended that you not mention this person. And if you go to different areas in your transcript -- ?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: At that time he said it, because at the same time he was also the Defence counsel of Mr. Pirkic Midhat, which I had not known. He advised me not to mention the name of this person in the Court. Actually I had a confrontation with Pirkic Midhat where I denied everything. First of all, I was afraid of Pirkic Midhat. If you knew him you would be afraid of him, too. That's first. Secondly, he said that if I don't mention his name, he will help me to get out, he will help me to avoid a sentence because I was a soldier executing the order, and he at that time had been the brigade commander in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And it was your lawyer that told to you make all these false statements, then.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: He advised me not to mention the name of Pirkic Midhat. And Mr. Delic Hazim -- well, let me answer you, since you asked me about these statements. I changed three or four statements at the Court at that time. And if you read them carefully enough you will see that I always try to avoid mentioning the name of the Delic Hazim. So there were a number of persons who influenced my statements at that time. If you read them carefully, you will see that. And the statements made to the Prosecutor where I blamed the Croats and not the Muslims. And I think this should be clear to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall saying in your statements to the office of the Prosecutor, and to help you along it's on page 50, starting about the middle of the page, talking about signing the statement, and Mrs. McHenry is asking you questions. And she says, "Why did you sign the 19" -- what did you have to -- in -- excuse me, "Why did you have to in 1994 sign the statement?" And your answer starts off, "And all this went through the lawyer who is defending me and who is defending the commander of the brigade, they had some accounts of their own". And then you went further on to say that, further down Mr. D'Hooge asked you if Mr. Delic told you what to put in your statement. And you responded, no, you were told to do that by your lawyer. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Sir, the statement I made to the Prosecutor is not entirely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: The statement made to which prosecutor, the one in Bosnia or Mrs. McHenry?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: The statement to the Prosecutor, here, and some statements I made in Bosnia. And during the day you will hear why they are not true, what is true, what is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, I think we will have to stop here and reassemble at 2.30 --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, first up, over the lunch break, did you discuss your testimony with anyone?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I did talk to my lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Nothing wrong with that, I just wanted to know. Mr. Landzo, I am going to change to a completely different subject. And I want to ask you about a comment you made in Court when you finished up your direct examination. You asked the presiding judge to be heard about some conditions in the detention unit. That you were being kept alone. Do you recall making that comment?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And that's nothing new, is it? Well, let me rephrase that, that was an unfair way to state it. When you first came to The Hague back in the summer of 1996, you were also kept away from the other defendants, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Not only me. We were all isolated. Each one of us went alone for a walk. We went alone for our gym exercise. I had a talk with Mr. McFaden. He has shown me a letter from the registry that I was to be in isolation for two weeks, due to the possible danger of me being injured by Mr. Mucic or Mr. Delic. At least that was the type of information I received, but you can check it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That was back in 1996, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, a few days ago when I began testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I want to focus on the time after you got to The Hague in 1996, okay. There was some period of time after that when, at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor, within the rules for detention, the registry ordered that you and the other defendants not be allowed to get together. You and these other three guys behind me; isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes. That was at the request of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And that continued for several months after you got here, didn't it? That you were kept alone and were kept isolated and weren't allowed to be around any other Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, a few months. And after those few months, I received the permission to meet with Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And after those few months, you were, we're talking that occurred when? October, November of 1996 that Judge Karibi-Whyte signed that order?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I have that piece of paper in the detention unit. I couldn't tell you just off.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But, you and the -- you were kept away from Mr. Landzo -- or, excuse me, Mr. Landzo, it's been a long day. You were kept away from Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delalic and Mr. Delic. Clearly beyond the 18th day of July, 1996; right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know how long I didn't have contact, but after a certain period, I could meet only with Mr. Delic. While with the other two accused, I had no contacts whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine. Let me go back to some of the other things we were talking about. Remember back in 1994 when you gave those statements to the Prosecutor's office back in Bosnia, the ones you say were somewhat true and not somewhat true? Do you remember those? We were talking about that right before lunch?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I do know that, I did give some statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And those were the ones that you said some of it's true and some of it's not true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: These statements were not completely true, but I can tell you the full truth here. I think we've all gathered here to seek out the truth and I can tell it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Sir, what I am getting at --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. He is not letting the defendant finish his statement. He said he'd like to tell the truth and Mr. Moran is cutting him off and not letting him finish his truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He his telling the truth. I think through his examination he will tell the truth. I suppose that's all it is meant to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And I am just trying to get you to confirm that those statements were not the whole truth. In fact, that's what you told Ms. McHenry and Mr. D'Hooge on the 18th of July, 1996?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: For a few statements. I know a certain truth. That Mr. Delic ordered me, that that person must be killed. I know that that was the truth. There are some other minor elements, which have been adjusted because some people asked me to adapt certain elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In fact, what you told Ms. McHenry and Mr. D'Hooge was not that Hazim told you to lie in your statement, but that your lawyer told you to do it, right? Your lawyer that represented you back in Bosnia, not Mr. Brackovic, but the lawyer that represented you back in Bosnia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, but we would have to go and seek out the background of it all in order to make it clear to the Trial Chamber and you, sir. For all of you who are interested in this, what really happened and how it happened. All this is connected with the statement. I think it would be necessary to furnish an explanation and I think we would save a lot of time, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you made those statements back in 1994, in Bosnia, the ones that you say that were not the whole truth, did you expect the officials of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to rely on the truthfulness of those statements or did you expect them to know that the statements you made under oath were untruthful?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: When I gave the last statement, which Madam Uzunovic asked me, "Landzo, who is sending you to change your statement?" Because I denied that. She asked me, "was it Delic, Hazim? Because in your statements, you never mention him and try to protect him." So the judge, inquiring judge, knew this and I didn't intend to lie. I didn't go many times alone, but Mr. Delic informed the guard that I would have to go to the Court and give a statement. And then the guard would come for me and tell me that I had to go to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you expected the officials of the Government of Bosnia, Herzegovina to rely on the truthfulness of those statements, did you not? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, I didn't expect it. They were bright enough to know what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So they knew that those statements you made under oath --

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, they weren't under oath, sir. That was still in the investigative stage. You can lie to the police or the inquiring judge. That was the general stand, both in Bosnia and in the former Yugoslavia, and those statements were not made under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, so it was okay to lie then, okay, that's fine. Let me go on to something else.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't all right. But I made those statements according to the advice I received from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So from your lawyer and you just testified a second ago --

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Lawyer, Mr. Delic and Mr. Mitko Pirkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And you said just a few seconds ago, I am reading the transcript." You can lie to the police or the inquiring judge." Okay, that's fine. Now, let me go on to something else. In July 1996, over in the jailhouse, you made a statement to Mrs. McHenry and Mr. D'Hooge. In fact, it's sitting right in front of you, the English version is sitting right in front of you. I understand your position now is that statement is not truthful; is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: It's not the complete truth. Well, but you will see that for yourself if you read it. And I stated that Mr. Delic was not a deputy commander of the camp, but just a guard. And, as you know, that's not true. And there are some other elements which are not true. And I am here to give the explanation and the truth to the Tribunal, to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just pick an example; Scepo Gotovac. When Mr. D'Hooge and Ms. McHenry ask you if you murdered that man, if you killed him, you denied it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, I denied that, but not only that, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I just picked that as an example, sir, okay.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: You can see also on the other counts that I denied everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That's right. And that was because of two reasons, right? You testified on page 15108 of the transcript, starting at line 7, about how when you were brought to Sarajevo, right before you came to The Hague, you were brought before a judge of the Supreme Court of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he made a statement to you. And the way you construed that statement starts at line 18 on page 15108. "Those who confess, half is given. Those who do not confess, will be forgiven everything. Which means, how I understood him that we should not confess anything that brought us here." Did you take that as advice from a justice of the Supreme Court of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be untruthful or just not to talk at all?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I listened to the advice of my -- the then Defence and I denied everything. And what the judge from the Supreme Court said in Sarajevo, I remember that. He told this in the entire story, but probably he meant something. But I wasn't led by this advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't take it as advice from a judge to lie, you just took it that it didn't mean anything or not to say anything?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I didn't say that the judge told me to lie, I just quoted his words. You can conclude what, but I listened to the advice of my then counsel and denied everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, so what the judge said didn't enter into your decision not to be truthful to Ms. McHenry and Mr. D'Hooge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He was acting on the advice of his counsel, this is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just want to make sure that no judicial officer in any country would have recommended that he would tell an untruth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I add an explanation? I know what the person said to Mr. Delic and myself and what the man looked like, but I don't know his name. I don't know whether that was a piece of advice or it was a sentence stated just like that. But I remember that he said and I construed a conclusion on the basis of that, what he wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And the conclusion was, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Not to admit to anything, confess any.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: It would have been a lot easier if you would have just said that a little while ago. Now, let's go on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to the side bar comments by Mr. Moran. They're uncalled for at this point. "It would have been a lot simpler if you had so earlier." That's intimidating the witness also.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, I am not trying to intimidate you. If you feel that I am intimidating you, let me know and I'll back off. Okay?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: You're doing your job and I have a duty here and, well, no offence meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, fine. We'll still be friends when it's over.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I certainly hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And then after you gave that statement on July the 18th, 1996, to the Office of the Prosecutor, there was a motion filed having to do with your competency to stand trial, you remember that? And because of that you were interviewed by probably more psychiatrists and psychologists than you ever wanted to see. You recall all those incidents? And you recounted some things in those statements to the psychiatrist that were not true, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes. Look, there were two reasons, as I have mentioned. My status at the time and the impossibility to remember everything. And I had an image in my head for which I considered to be true. And we must return to my Defence at the time who chose this tactics for my Defence. You should ask him why he chose that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Oh, we will. But, so the Defence at the time was that you were insane at the time of the crime, is that it? And that you, therefore, could not be held criminally responsible, is that what the Defence was?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. He is asking the defendant to come to a legal conclusion and that's not something that he is aware of. He knows that the statute says lack of mental capacity and diminished mental capacity. I doubt if he knows what the legal definition of insanity is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he knows what his Defence was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, he says, we must return to my Defence at the time who chose the tactics. Well, I want to know what the tactics were and I want to know what the Defence was and I think I am entitled to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: The Defence at the time was that you were not criminally responsible because of your mental condition; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, you should ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I just did what I was told to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And so you simulated inability to remember things, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: As I have said, I didn't simulate intentionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: This was my condition at the time. And I believe that all that I know, everything is the truth, but much of it is not the truth. But at the time this was the truth for me and I believed in that. And I would talk about it to anyone who asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Sir, a couple of weeks ago, somewhere around the 3rd of July, do you recall talking to Dr. Lagazzi?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And he wrote a report that's in evidence as D 63/4. And, in that report, Dr. Lagazzi wrote, and I will read it to you or we'll get it for you and you can read it yourself. Dr. Lagazzi wrote on page 8, "On some occasions (as he now admits) he simulated disorders of awareness and orientation which were not compatible with the clinical reality of the case." Now, did Dr. Lagazzi just make that up or did he have some basis for saying that you simulated those or can you explain why Dr. Lagazzi would have that in his report if you didn't tell him that you simulated that lack of orientation?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I believe I know what you were speaking about. He asked me what the day is and what is the season. At the time, in fact, I wasn't going out. And I didn't have a watch. I didn't have a calendar. And I couldn't tell him. And if he concluded that I was simulating, well, he is a professional. Maybe he could, under these conditions, conclude that. But, I told him what I believed was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: And that he concluded that I was simulating, he will be able to tell you more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And on page 3 of his report, if you recall, there was a translation error. And --

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I didn't say there was a translation error, I just said what I had told him, I don't know how he understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Well, if you recall back when we were upstairs in that other courtroom and I was chatting with Dr. Lagazzi like I am chatting with you now, I asked him about a portion of his report, on page 3 of his report, and he said there was a translation error. And the translation is in the sentence, he emphasised -- he being you -- emphasised that he was not mad. And here's where the translation error is. The printed report says that he at no time simulated apparent temporal and spatial disorientation, as he had been recommended to do so. And, as I recall, what Dr. Lagazzi said was that you did admit it. And the next sentence says, He -- meaning you -- maintains that he only later understood that such an attitude was useless and counterproductive and he is, therefore, critical of his previous Defence counsel who persuaded him to make the wrong decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object because I can't understand the question. I believe there might have been three questions at one time. And if you could break it down, I believe it's a compound question and I don't believe that the defendant should be forced to try to follow that line of thinking right now. Could you simplify it? .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did the witness understand the question? If he did not, he will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What I was asking about if you remembered when Dr. Lagazzi talked about the translation in the paragraph that I read to you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't remember it exactly. I know that he, in his testimony spoke about his last report along maybe these lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And he said he simulated this, he would have just been mistaken or wrong, is that what your position is, Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I can't say what he thought, I am just telling you what I said at that time. It may be true that I said this to him, I can't recall everything, but I know that I told Dr. Lagazzi everything on the occasion of our last interview about everything. And I told him why there was a discrepancy between certain statements. I gave him the reasons -- well, I don't know exactly whether I said what you emphasised, but if this is what Dr. Lagazzi wrote down, then I guess this is what I had said, but I cannot recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Landzo, there were only three people at that meeting. One was an interpreter, one was Dr. Lagazzi, and one was you; and all I am relying on is what Dr. Lagazzi said in his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object, that is a misstatement. There were two interpreters. It had to go from Dutch to Italian, and Italian to Bosnian, so there were four people present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there were four people present, two interpreters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry Mr. Landzo, there were four people present. Two interpreters, and you, and Dr. Lagazzi. So all we have to rely on is what you tell us and what Dr. Lagazzi tells us, isn't that right? On what you said.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, that is up to you to conclude. I don't claim that I am right on everything. I am just talking to you about the things I recall, and Dr. Lagazzi probably wrote down in his statement what he heard and what he recalls. It may very well be that I said something I cannot recall or that he put down something that he didn't understand well, I don't know that, you should ask the gentleman, you should ask the two interpreters, because there was really two interpreters there. There was one translating from Serbo-Croatian into Dutch and the other from Dutch into Italian, so I really don't know. And you see when interpreting is being done, it is not every word that is interpreted. And if you have two interpreters, of course you have two different languages and they, perhaps, will not use the same words.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Sure. And it could have been an interpretation problem and Dr. Lagazzi may just have gotten mixed up, that's fine. Let's go back on to some of the other things you told me.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: It may very well be that I said something there, but I cannot recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine, Mr. Landzo. Now, that was what? The third time? Or the third sequence of times that Dr. Lagazzi interviewed you, right? The first two times were in 1996?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Late 1996, maybe early 1997. When you talked to Dr. Lagazzi, those first times, you told him some things that were not true, didn't you? Well, let me give you an example.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. You told him, for instance, that you were mixing pills and alcohol. And that wasn't true, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's already been covered. Why keep on repeating yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just want to ask him a couple of things about that. Actually, the biggest thing I wanted to ask you about that was, you lied about that because your lawyer, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Inaudible)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: First of all, I was told in this Court in 1997 not to call the witness a liar. And I object that Mr. Moran is calling the witness a liar at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I misspoke, I'm sorry, that statement was untruthful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He already said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And the reason for your untruthfulness was because you were told to do that by your lawyer?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I told you that on a number of occasions before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And that, presumably, was to aid in your Defence. There were some other statements that were made about that time that were not correct to Dr. Lagazzi. There was the statement about -- what other things you did tell him back then that were not truthful, let's just start with that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: If you give me the report, I will specify to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we want, we can do that or we can move on. It's the Court's pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have exhausted those things in regards to inaccuracies, move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, would it surprise you if I told you that last night after you essentially waived the attorney/client privilege with Mr. Brackovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object, has the Court ruled that that attorney/client privilege has been totally waived from Mr. Brackovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Who is objecting to it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am objecting on behalf of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's not a privilege between you and him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It is a privilege between my client and his former attorney and I believe it is my duty to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me hear your submission that he is volunteering what he told you is privileged. Let's hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Are you asking me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let the person objecting make the submission. But after volunteering what went on between the witness and counsel, that statement is still privileged.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: All I am asking is that there be a ruling that the attorney/client privilege has been waived, so that either it's clear that it has or it's clear that it hasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If the witness volunteers whatever he told his counsel, the privilege no longer holds. If there was a privilege, he would have been the one to plead it. And he would not have said it at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: My only concern here is that as his advocate, he may not know about the privilege, and I think it's my duty to object when it appears that some damage may be done to him. But if the privilege has been waived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: After extensively speaking on the privilege, to your knowledge, you were sitting down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure it was waived or not waived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: After it's all been stated, you would have stopped him doing it at that time. It was your responsibility to have warned him that he should not do it, but you did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think we discussed it two days ago, Your Honour, I just wanted to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You knew what he did. 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Far too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour, I'm just about set to wind it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Would it surprise you, sir, if I were to tell you that when Mr. Karabdic was speaking to Mr. Brackovic on the telephone last night, Mr. Brackovic was asked about the Croatian death camp you talked about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object, number one; this is total hearsay and he has to prove the reliability of these statements. He is talking about Mr. Karabdic's conversation with Mr. Brackovic. If Mr. Moran had it, that's one thing, but we don't have any party here to this interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you are right here. You don't have to introduce matters which are completely irrelevant. We have no idea about what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And so, you made these false statements in 1996 and 1997 to the psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Statements that were incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And now you're here telling the truth; is that what you're saying, Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, if you should be surprised with that, I don't see any problem here. Because I am aware of the responsibilities emanating from my lying here, if I should lie here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, so, we should believe you now, even though those other statements were not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I'm not asking anybody to believe me, but just to listen to my story, to what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any questions from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think Mr. Moran has --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me first do a couple of housekeeping matters with the usher's assistance. Mrs. McMurrey yesterday introduced a letter from Mr. Landzo to the office of the Prosecutor, and I now have the responses to Mr. Landzo and to his counsel. And just for purposes of completeness, I would ask that they be accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You did not apply to him. You must pass it on to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: There was both, Your Honour, you can see that both Mr. Landzo was replied to and counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If that's what it says, because where it was said he should be given death sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's the letter. And just for purposes of completeness, I'm not going to go into it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it's, let's have the full cycle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want the record to be clear that we have not insinuated that there was any impropriety on the part of the Prosecution. So we have certainly no objections to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is no such insinuation at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The second matter, just with the assistance of the usher, there is a matter that was discussed in private session yesterday and something was redacted. At some later point the Prosecution is going to discuss that matter and argue that it not be redacted. I previously gave Defence counsel earlier this morning copies of some material already in evidence that we will be relying upon to show the relevance of the material. And just so that Your Honours have it now, I just -- .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That incident is not part of the indictment at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And evidence with regard to that might prejudice the case of the accused. That is why we said, redact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I did not argue, we did not object at the time because we had not had a full opportunity to review the record. I'm not planning on arguing it now, but at some later point during the testimony, after Your Honours have had an opportunity to review what's already in the record, I will be arguing that that matter is relevant, at least for some limited purposes. And so, for now all I'm doing is providing the Court the portions of the record that I will later be relying upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why don't you wait until that stage before you introduce it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Because we're not sure whether it will be admitted at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The gentleman who was killed in that incident was also detainee in Celebici camp. I think that is evidence. And that gentleman, we have not included in the indictment at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are not -- the matter that I'm discussing does not have to do with the Bubalo issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought it was in reference to that incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, it's not in reference to that incident. Thank you

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I know you don't know the exact date that you started working in Celebici, but you would agree it was some 7 to 10 days after the fall of Bradina; correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I think it was mid-June, maybe the first half of June, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that when you were in Celebici, Mr. Mucic ordered that the rifles of the guards be kept cocked, ready to fire at all times?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Delic insisted on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you've already stated that Mr. Mucic was in charge of the camp. Who was in charge of the camp when Mr. Mucic was not present?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Mr. Delic. When both were not present, then the guard service commander, Sejo Mustafic was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you have more authority than other guards or different kinds of authority, or just exactly the same authority as other guards?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: The same authority, like all other guards. I was not different from the others in any way. I was doing everything that the others were doing, I had the same orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Could any guard call a prisoner out of a hangar, or just certain guards?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Any guard who was on duty, on the mound, above hangar 6. I was not always there. We would be on duty for a certain period of time, and whoever was on duty would be then called in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And then is it correct that when you were not on duty, you could not call a prisoner out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I could if I had an order of either the commander or his deputy to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned something yesterday, or Monday, about a knife which was given to an Arab TV crew. Can you tell me about that knife and the circumstances under which it was given to the TV crew?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: The knife was found behind the belt, I think, of the person that allegedly had killed Muslims in the second World War, it was found on him. I asked Delic whether I could have the knife. He said yes, and I kept it as a souvenir. It was a knife going back to the second World War. And when a TV crew, whether it was Arab or not I really don't know, Mr. Delic took this knife from me and gave it to them. It was a very small knife.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And was Celebici visited on more than one occasion by TV crews?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Once, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And is that when some Arab journalists came?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Possibly they were Arabs, but I just saw people, individuals. I wasn't present when they were talking, in order to be able to conclude who they were and where they were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that at least a few people were released from Celebici during the time that you were there. Do you know if two detainees named Vojislav Sinikovic and Vladimir Sinikovic were released when you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know the names, but there were two brothers, and Redzo Balic came and a neighbour came to pick them up in order to exchange these two for Redzo's brother. And I know that Redzo came with a car and a tire blew out, and they had to change it. So, these were two persons who were rather tall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And do you know on whose authority those people were released? Or did you ever see any documents related to their release?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. McMurrey talked to you about counts 46 and 47 of the indictment, dealing with inhumane conditions, and she asked you some questions about food. Now, the detainees would bring the food from the administration building to the area right in front of hangar 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes. Two detainees would go from the hangar with a guard, they would take and receive the food from the administration building and in front of the hangar they would be distributing the food to detainees who would be coming out in groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And the detainees would come out in groups of five, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know that these were groups between five and ten, something like that. They would hold these, they would have their plate, plates, and they would be sitting in front of the hangar on the floor, or they would be just kneeling down and eating.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And they only had a few minutes to eat; didn't they, each group?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Well, the time wasn't limited. They could eat it as long -- they had the portion, there was no need to rush them. They had their rations and they could eat it as long as they wished. In five minutes or longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you stated in, when you testified here this week, that the prisoners got the same amount of food as the guards. You would agree with me in your prior statement to the office of the Prosecutor, you stated that the prisoners may have gotten less food. Do you remember that? And if so, what's changed your mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Read the whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The question you were asked, "What about the food that was given to the detainees?" And you said, "We got the same food. The same food was given to the prisoners and the guards. The food was the same. It may have been less because there were so many."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question used the word "may", Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: "We got what we got, that was distributed." Do you remember giving that answer before?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, the ratio of food for us and for detainees, we were 25, 30, guards, we received a certain quantity, while they were in 250 or 300 detainees. Their quantities were much bigger in total. But the same food came in, but of course, the quantities could have been different. But we couldn't decide about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, would you agree that the quantities may have been less for the prisoners, for each individual prisoner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Possibly, possibly. I was looking when they were, they were distributing, they would get a ladle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, going to the tunnel, about 40 persons were kept in tunnel number 9; weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Approximately, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And there was a bucket that was used for human waste for when the detainees could not go outside to use the toilet inside tunnel number 9; wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I didn't know, wasn't acquainted with the situation inside hangar number 9. I knew better what the situation was in hangar number 6. I was there more frequently, and at the gate.

utterances.speaker: MRS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness be shown Defence Exhibit 9/4? I have extra copies with some English translations on them for the judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, that was an exhibit that was previously shown to witnesses from your counsel. That's a drawing you made; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that in tunnel number 9 you've drawn something and said that that's where the human waste pail is; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection as to whether or not tunnel number 9 had a human waste pail in it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: These drawings were drawn on the basis of the statements of the witnesses. I knew, on the basis of that, I knew where they were sitting, and I made this drawing on the basis of the statement. But I haven't seen the bucket. Possibly it existed, but I have not seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, the prisoners kept in tunnel 9 were considered to have been the leaders of the Serbs, the local Serbs, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes. And the organisers of the rebellion, and the most dangerous ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. McMurrey read out to you parts of counts 46 and 47, to you, dealing with inhumane conditions. But she didn't read out the part about the atmosphere of terror created by the killing and abuse of other detainees. Sir, you would agree that you participated in the existence of an atmosphere of terror in the Celebici camp; wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, I was executing orders. I wasn't the one to be able to decide whether somebody should be beaten or not. There were also other guards who did these things, and I was not present. So, if we want to speak about it, we could say that everybody who was in Celebici influenced the creation of such an atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, your statement would be that you didn't, you're not the only person who participated in the existence of an atmosphere of terror, but you were certainly one of the persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would also agree with me, wouldn't you, that in 1992 there were many reports in Konjic, in the town, about the mistreatment in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Many reports?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: People talking in town about the mistreatment in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about it, but I would rarely come from Celebici to Konjic. It's possible that there were, because Celebici is not far from Konjic. It wasn't hidden, concealed so that nobody would know about it. And then many other guards went home, maybe they spoke and talked about it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, maybe I can refresh your recollection. Do you remember in your previous statement to the office of the Prosecutor, you mentioned the reports about mistreatment several times, and let me just read you one part. Question: "I believe you mentioned before that there were many reports in town about mistreatment of prisoners; is that right?" Answer, "Yes". Question, "Can you tell us about these reports and how widespread they were?" Answer, "It wasn't so much widespread, but it originated from the people who came into the camp to beat the prisoners and then spread stories that we were doing it." Question, "And how did you hear about those stories?" Answer, "I heard about these stories when I went home, and my mother asked me what we were doing there." Question, "This is while you were still at the camp; is that right?" Answer, "Yes".

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, my mother did ask me, but nobody in town would stop me and ask me what are you doing there. But I don't know from where my mother heard that. And this statement is not completely exact. But I heard that the guard, later on, that the guards who were participating in this talked about it. But I heard about that only after joining the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me go through a number of specific events. And I'll tell you right now that I'm not going to go over in detail the murders and tortures that you remember committing and already testified about, since there is no dispute about them, but I have a few questions about some of them. And I have some questions about some events that you haven't remembered. First, you testified yesterday and Monday about when you and some others murdered Mr. Scepo Gotovac; did you and the other guards use any instruments to kill him or did you just beat and kick him to death?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I think that one of them had a police baton. Well, the others had their weapons, their personal weapons on them. And when the beating began it was dark, and the man was the ground. So, it was very difficult to see who was beating with what, hitting with what.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember, before the final beating, had Mr. Gotovac ever been beaten before, to your knowledge, while in Celebici? If you don't remember, you can say you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know that he came already beaten up to our camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And my question is, do you -- ?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't remember. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the final beating, do you remember everyone else who was participating in or present during the beating besides any detainees?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know that we were five of us, but I really can't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, let's talk for a minute about a killing where you had not received orders, and you talked in detail about before the killing you had gone to view some murders in an area near Repovci, and you heard that some Serbs from Bradina had done it. Now at some later point you heard it was not Serbs that had killed the people in Repovci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: That is what is being, that's the word that's being spread now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that on your way back to Celebici camp from Repovci you tried to capture a Serb woman to kill her, too, but she got away?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: This didn't happen. I can't recall it happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
