utterances.text: You stated when you got back to Celebici you and about eleven other people started beating two detainees until finally Mr. Delic stopped the beatings. What was the name of the detainees, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know that they were the ones who would regularly distribute food. One I've seen on the video, one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember their names, or not?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then you indicated you were still angry so you went to hangar 6 and told all the Serbs from Bradina to stand up. You would agree with me you wanted to hurt someone and you wanted that person to be a Serb from Bradina; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Do you mean -- you see, I was angry, angry on what I've seen and what I've heard, and this was my reaction. I didn't come there with the intention of killing anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that you wanted to hurt someone, and you wanted that person to be a Serb from Bradina, to take out your anger. That would be a fair statement; wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: This is how you could put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, the person you killed, his name was Bosko Samoukovic; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, I was the cause of his death, but I didn't go there with the intent to kill him. Yes, that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And what did you use to beat him?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: There was a plank, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you use your right or your left hand when you beat him?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Left. Not just when I was beating him. There were two or three before him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, did I understand you to say that you can't remember exactly how Mr. Samoukovic got to the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know how he did. I told you that I think I ordered two or three detainees and together with them we took him to the infirmary. He could walk, but we were carrying him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And so he was carried rather than driven, you're sure about that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, not as far as I can recall it. He was actually carried on the hands that were clinched underneath him by two detainees, so he was sitting on their hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, what happened after you killed Mr. Samoukovic? In other words, was there any kind of report that you made? Did you talk to anyone about this? Did anybody ask you about it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: At the time when we were still in the infirmary, I was standing at door while he was examined by the doctors, Hazim Delic came to the infirmary to see what happened because there was a number of other guards that gathered there. He started raising hell, shouting at me. And after about an hour I was summoned to his office and he told me that he had to yell at me in front of these other guards and "Who fucks his mother", sorry I have to use these words, he said, "Fuck his mother, you should have killed him."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Going to another death in Celebici, Mr. Slavko Susic. Is the only time you saw Mr. Susic in Celebici camp when you were bringing him to tunnel nine and you hit him just a few times? Did you ever see him in Celebici at any other time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No. I cannot recall it. Maybe I happened to be there when I was off duty and when they were getting out I could have seen him. Next to tunnel 9 there was always a guard. In the morning two, three guards would come who were off duty to help this guard next to tunnel 9 to take the detainees out to the toilet, to the washing area, and I may have happened to be there, but, and see him, but I can't recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, the occasion that you do remember, you stated that other persons, guards, were hitting him with a bat and with sticks. Can you tell us what kind of bat and what kind of sticks were being used by the other persons?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: One was hitting him with a police baton, and the others were hitting him by hands, because it was a very narrow area, there was not room enough for any larger object to be used for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, do you remember everyone who was present or participating in this beating of Mr. Susic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I think there was a guard who was called Focak, the others I do not know. Focak was a very hefty man, so I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you saying that right now you don't remember who the other people were, or are you saying that at the time you didn't know who they were?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I can't remember it now. I probably knew these people, if they were guards, but I can't recall their names right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember, was this during the day or night?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I think it was about five, 6.00 p.m. when he was brought in. I think that was the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you would certainly agree that your hand and your asthma did not prevent you from killing Mr. Gotovac and Mr. Samoukovic, did it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I did not kill. I did not kill. Are you talking about Susic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I have gone on to a different question. I am just -- I take it you would agree -- well, let me just move on. Now, I would like to talk to you about Mr. Simo Jovanovic. Now, your testimony is that you are called him out of the hangar and you helped bring him back to the hangar, but that you didn't actually beat him yourself, is that correct? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now who was it who actually beat him?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know that those were the guards who came from the Idbar village. I know one who had this large gavel that you use to beat meat. He would carry it around. And the next day he said that he would use the gavel and hit him on his head and everywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now you say when these people first came, these other guards, and asked for Simo Jovanovic, you were supposed to call them out. Why is it that the other guards didn't call them out themselves? Why did they need you to call Mr. Jovanovic out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Because he was not allowed to have contact with detainees because he was not on duty. It was my duty to communicate with the detainees, since I was the guard on duty there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I thought you said just a few minutes ago that if someone had an order from the commander or the deputy commander, the guard could call someone out of the hangar themselves, even when they weren't on duty or on post?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: He would get the order. He would ask the person on the guard post to call up the person, the detainee, that is. If I was not on duty, I couldn't do it. It had to be done by the guard on duty on that guard post. Of course, if I had been ordered to do it, I would then take over such a detainee who would have come out, but I couldn't call him up unless I was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And do you remember testifying differently just a few minutes ago about that issue?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't explain it well enough, but that's how it was. That's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when these people first came and asked for Mr. Jovanovic, you thought they were going to beat him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I assumed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: But I couldn't do anything. I couldn't prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you could hear the beating from where you were inside your guard shelter and -- that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you stated that the beating lasted about twenty minutes and you could hear the beating and you could hear the shouts. Could you hear Mr. Jovanovic begging for his life?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Maybe. I know that I heard voices, but I can't recall the words. I heard voices. I heard swearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to turn to something else, sir. Mr. Nedeljko Draganic, on how many occasions was Mr. Draganic beaten, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: You mean by the other guards?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am asking just how many times that you know of that he was beaten in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I was present once, maybe I was present on some other occasions when he was beaten up, but the rest I don't know. Because I really didn't know everything that was going on there. When I was on duty and what I was told to do, I know about. But what were the orders given to the other guards, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you stated you remembered hitting Mr. Spasoje Miljevic once. And on another occasion you burned his leg so that he would not be able to walk, do you also remember burning his hand with a heated knife, similar to what you did with Momir Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't recall it really.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He never said he burned Momir Kuljanin with a knife, I don't believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe he did say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, it's correct isn't it, that you did and you testified that you burned Mr. Momir Kuljanin with a knife?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise, I am incorrect in that, I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a metal object. Whether it was a knife or not, I don't know. But I know that it was a metal object.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you can't recall if you similarly burned Mr. Miljevic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: If I had done it, I would certainly remember it just as I can remember the former incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: He could walk afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to Mirko Babic, you said you didn't know who he was, but you would agree with me that in 1996, when you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you were quite positive about who Mr. Babic was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Could you please read my statement to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, certainly. Do you know -- and I am going to read portions of this. I am starting on page 80, portions of the transcript of how you know him. There are other discussions about what happened to him that I won't read now. You were asked, "do you know anything about the treatment of Mirko Babic?" And you said, "I know that when he was brought in, he was beaten." You were asked, "do you know who it is?" And you answered, "yes." And then later on, you were asked, "what was the age of Mirko Babic?" And you said, "40 to 50, middle-aged." You were then asked if you knew him from before and you said, "no." And you were specifically asked, "how do you remember this person?" And you stated, "I know when they took his personal information, he had a moustache." You were then asked, "you just remember that from mentioning his name that one time?" And you answered, "yes, when they would come out in the morning, I knew who he was." Does that refresh your recollection about the fact in 1996 you did know who Mirko Babic was?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: It may very well be that I confused him for another person. I really didn't know who Mirko Babic was until he arrived here to testify as a witness. That was the first time I saw him and I thought, perhaps, I could recall this person, but it may be very well be that I confused him for another person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I mean, I am really not sure. I believe that this is what I said, but it may very well have been that I have confused him with someone else because many of such people were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me talk for a minute about the women in the camp. It's correct, isn't it, that you believe that the women in the camp were all civilians?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: You mean personally I thought they were?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I couldn't fathom it that women of that age could have been members of a military unit. I had, earlier had an opportunity to see women, but they were younger, who were members of the military unit. I was not sure, that was my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And, in fact, you believe that the reason Mrs. Cecez was in the camp was because her husband was thought to be a leader of the Serbs, correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: That was the story.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the treatment of Mrs. Cecez or Mrs. Antic when they were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I heard stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And, in fact, was it generally reported in the camp that they had been raped while they were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I didn't hear that at that time. I heard it in the course of the year 1994, '96 from Mr. Delic what was going on with these women. But, at that time, nobody was really speaking about it. I personally heard no one to that effect, except the case that I witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Delic tell you about the treatment of Mrs. Cecez and Mrs. Antic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: That they were raped.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Delic tell you anything about who raped them?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: He said that he raped them and he was bragging about it when we were at the Zenica prison. He would tell this to everyone who wanted to listen him. And everyone knew him there as a person who slept with 600 women.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now have a question about a sexual assault victim whose identity has not been made public and I would ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: (In open session).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that after the beatings -- and, I'm sorry, after, when you saw the murdered people in Repovci, you were ordered to interrogate the Djordic brothers, which you did. Who told you that you should interrogate the Djordic brothers?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, that Mr. Mucic told you in interrogating the Djordjic brothers that you should use every possible way to interrogate them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: He may have said this, I don't recall it. He just told me, I know that to take statements from them, oral or written.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me show you something, sir, and see if it refreshes your recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 263.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would like to know if the Defence is going to be given a copy of it, so we know what it is that we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, I did supply extra copies. It has previously been provided to defence, but, right, there are extra copies now that the usher can give you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is this the document you provided at lunch time today or the first break?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, this is the document provided many months ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have found the section in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And, sir, does that refresh your recollection about whether or not Mr. Mucic ordered you to question the Djordjics in every possible way?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Maybe. But, if I may, I would like to explain statement, may I?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, at this point, you don't need to explain the statement, you can just say whether it does or does not refresh your recollection about whether or not Mr. Mucic told you to use every possible way?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. She has placed the statement before him and has asked him to explain it and she is saying that he can't. And will the Court allow him to respond to the statement that's been placed before him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Put your question and let him explain what he tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you can explain it, but can you first tell me whether or not this document refreshes your recollection as to whether or not Mr. Mucic told you to use every possible way in interrogating the Djordjic brothers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Initially when you asked him the question, he couldn't recollect that right as to the taking of the statements. All he knew he was asked to take statements. That was what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He stated he did not remember if Mr. Mucic said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You're now taking him back to his statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: To justify that he might have said such a thing. This is what he wants to explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't recall it, whether Mucic said it or not. But this statement here, I think that there is another statement, unless I am wrong. This was made in connection with the indictment issued against Mucic, Zdravko, and Ivica at the military court in Konjic. And I was asked, I think that Mr. Delic too was asked to make statements concerning the acts committed by Mucic because he was a Croat. And, at that time, there was a conflict, a clash actually, between the BiH army and the HVO. So it may very well be true, but I can't recall exactly what he had told me. I just know that he had told me to take a written or oral statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And was this the only time that Mr. Mucic asked you to take statements or were there other occasions where Mr. Mucic also asked you to take statements?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Only this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And did Mr. Mucic indicate to you why he chose you to take these statements from the Djordjic brothers?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, it's correct, isn't it, that as part of taking the statement, you did mistreatment the Djordjic brothers, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree that you mistreated them, but it wasn't part of their interrogation; is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: When I was interviewing them, I did not beat them. They were beaten up on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, you would agree that you, yourself, mistreated the Djordjic brothers, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes. When Mr. Delic came to the hangar together with me, if you're referring to that incident, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And is it your testimony, sir, that when you put the fuse on Mr. Djordjic and when you made them perform oral sex, it was unrelated to their interrogation? Is that what you believed?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, no, that happened after the incident in the administration building with Mr. Nimic. That happened afterwards. And I think that nobody interrogated them afterwards or talked to them about these events in Repovci while they were staying in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think, Mrs. McHenry, we might break now and come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mrs. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, in 1992 you knew that Mr. Mucic was Zejnil Delalic's right hand man, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I told that to you, but I didn't know it for, as a certainty. I heard that from Mitko Pirkic. I'm not sure, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, there was a written notice posted in Celebici from Mr. Zejnil Delalic concerning who had authority to enter Celebici camp; wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know that there was an oral order by Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember in 1996, after you were indicted, but before you were arrested, giving an interview to a Bosnian newspaper?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do recollect that I gave the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you were reported, sir, in that interview, to have indicated that if Mr. Delalic learned that a guard had mistreated prisoners, he would have the guards sent to the front-line, and that there was a written order from Mr. Delalic posted in the camp concerning who had authority to enter the camp. Do you remember saying those things when you gave your interview in 1996?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I never said that. I gave an explanation. I gave my statement to the prosecutors what was the situation, and I can repeat that, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Maybe just -- and the explanation you gave in your interview with the office of the Prosecutor was that you did give an interview, that they correctly reported everything you said, except for the part dealing with Mr. Delalic. And is that still your testimony, sir, that everything else was correct, and everything else correctly stated what you said to the journalists, and it was only the part about Mr. Delalic that you didn't say to the journalists?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just ask for the assistance of the defendant if he could please be shown a copy of this document to refresh his memory? I don't know that any of us have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It was an exhibit to his statement and given that the witness appears to remember it without any problem, I don't think it's necessary. Of course, if the witness asks for it, I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any questions on that statement, if you're not correct what he has said, it I think it might not be necessary. But you can explain to him what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree, when asked about this article in your interview with the office of the Prosecutor, you agreed that you gave the interview, and you indicated that everything in the article correctly represented what you had said with the exception of the part dealing with Mr. Delalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You might as well show him that aspect.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know that they were asking me about the structure of the prison, how the guards function, and at one point they asked me about Zejnil Delalic, but I couldn't say anything about that person. But they were mainly focusing on the events in Celebici. And at that time I didn't say anything about Zejnil Delalic, and I was surprised when I saw that article. I haven't seen it prior to that occasion when you've shown it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Because it's already discussed in your interview with the office of the Prosecutor, I don't believe it's necessary to take the time to go through it. Let me move on to another matter. Sir, when witnesses, Prosecution witnesses have been in the courtroom, you and other accused have made threatening comments to the witnesses; haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Mucic and myself, we only talked about that, but I didn't threaten anyone. I think I made a comment that listening to all that has been said and that I had done all that has been stated here, I would feel less guilty, I would feel better than to listen to all that has happened and that which has not happened. Remembering that. But somebody else interpreted that differently, and that's the way it turned out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, sir, is it your testimony that when Witness J was on the stand that you did not raise your voice and say you wanted to lie him on concrete and step on him not one time but a million times?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you aware of any improper efforts made by any accused in this case to tell Defence witnesses exactly what they should say when they testify?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Do you, you're asking if I know about such attempts?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you aware of any improper efforts or attempts?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I just commented for myself, I don't know what others did. I analyse all the witnesses, be it from the Defence or for the Prosecution. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it a fair statement that you can't even remember all the times you beat, mistreated or tortured detainees in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know whether I hit somebody once or five times, but if I beat somebody severely, or killed somebody, I think that I could remember that. But I cannot remember if I kicked one somebody. But if some bigger things occurred, that, yes, maybe not immediately in the beginning, but after all that has been stated in front of the Court, I think that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, let's then talk about some potentially bigger incidents. Can you remember all the times that you burned people, either by setting them on fire, setting their clothes on fire, putting a burning fuse around them? Can you remember all those instances?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know, I remember Spasoje Miljevic, and Kuljanin, Momir Kuljanin. That is where I perpetrated that, while for the others, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjic, you testified about when you burned him.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And my question, sir, is: Can you remember if there were any other occasions when you burned people?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, but probably I would remember if that had occurred. To tell you the truth, I didn't remember even these three cases when I arrived here in 1996. I didn't remember them. But I can say with, state with certainty that I participated in these events. While for the others, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, what kind of instruments, besides police batons, sticks, fuses and setting people on fire, what other kinds of instruments were used by you and the other persons in Celebici to mistreat the detainees?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I generally kicked with my feet because I couldn't do it with my hands. Others used, for example, a baseball bat, then parts of chairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How about gas masks?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know that they were in the warehouse under lock and key.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that the gas masks were sometimes used on detainees; wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know, it's possible. But if you ask me what I know, I don't know about that. Because I repeat, I wasn't the only guard there. You should verify with all, check with all guards what was happening. And I didn't do it, didn't use it, and I didn't have any access to these gas masks, they were under lock and key in Building D.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And now, sir, is it your testimony that you never heard of gas masks being used against detainees when you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Possibly I heard it then, in Celebici, but I don't remember now. Many events took place throughout the day or at night, and then I would hear these stories the next day. I didn't give them much importance. And then with time, this is forgotten, particularly if I wasn't in, on the spot where this was happening. I have experienced many, many things from 1992 until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me see if this refreshes your recollection, sir. Prosecution Exhibit 263, which is the statement you gave about the Djordjic brothers that you were shown a few minutes ago; in it you talk about how you put a gas mask on their heads and when they had no air, I took the mask off and continued questioning them. Sir, is it your testimony that you just put that in there about gas masks, even though you didn't know anything about them being used by you or other people in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Maybe I stated it, but I don't remember it. I know that the gas masks existed in Celebici and that they were in the warehouse. And I really don't know whether anybody used them, but I know that I didn't use them. But this statement, and these were statements against Mucic Zdravko and Mucic (sic) Ivica because it was the idea to put all the blame on the Croats. I mentioned already that many of these statements, allegations are not true. I was at the time in prison when giving these statements. I was in prison when I was giving this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me ask you, do you remember participating in any false executions, where you would pretend to a detainee that you were going to shoot him, although in fact you did not ultimately shoot him? Do you remember you or anyone else participating in false executions?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I know -- .

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, we have a problem with the transcript, line 19 used the word Mucic, when the used the word Buric. B-U-R-I-C I-V-I-C-A.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: On one occasion I wasn't on duty, and three of us, on orders of Mr. Delic, we came in front of hangar 6. He brought out a person by the surname of Kuljanin, I believe that the person surname was Kuljanin. He brought him out, and he ordered him to stand in front of that mound. There was a drainage channel. And while for the three of us to stand in one line, as if we would be falsely executing him. And Delic gave us orders how to prepare and cock the guns. I remember that case in which I was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were prisoners ever placed in manholes?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Tell us what you know about when prisoners were placed in manholes, Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I remember when a prisoners from tunnel number 9 were taken, all the guards were accompanying this group of detainees from tunnel 9 to that manhole, we accompanied them, they were on one side, we on the other. I believe that Mr. Mucic, I'm not sure that he was present, but I know that Mr. Delic was certainly present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember if prisoners were ever made to drink urine?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember cigarettes ever being put out in detainees hands?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I didn't do it. I never smoked cigarettes, and I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you were ordered to torture and even kill prisoners, and sometimes other guards received similar orders. Do you know if all the other guards were ordered to mistreat prisoners, or was it just some guards?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I, while I was at the guard position at hangar 6 I could hear the noises of hits, beatings, shouts, and somebody else was doing that. That was my conclusion. So, I believe others received orders, because sometimes I would come on guard duty in the morning and I would see that there are beaten persons. I don't know, however, if they had the order, but I assumed they did have the orders to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, would you agree with me that there were some guards, not the majority, but some guards who did not mistreat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I can't recall it. At the time when I was there, I can't recall this sort of guards. Maybe afterwards, because I just spent a month-and-a-half, and when I left, other guards would come. I heard from stories in town that new guards would come in, maybe they did it. Let me just tell you that one person among the guards, Mustafic Sejo, I think was his name, was the only person that didn't do it. He was in charge of receiving the food, distributing the food, while all the others, more or less, took part in it. On one occasion, there were 15 guards that would beat up a detainee.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And was that on orders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How would he know?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, because Mr. Delic was present on that occasion. And when this detainee was beaten, he caused an injury to his leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you present on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who was the detainee, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Zeljko Ceces, called "Spanac."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were Samir Hondo, Sarif Pajic or Senad Omerka, do you know if they were guards when you were Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Samir Hondo was there while I was at Celebici. Omerka I'm not sure. I can't recall whether he was there at the time I was at Celebici. I saw him later on the videotape, he was a refugee and he lived in that part of Celebici next to the camp. But I cannot really tell you whether he was there at the time when I was at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever see Samir Hondo mistreat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Not me personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: As far as you know nothing bad happened to Sejo Mustafic and Samir Hondo in Celebici camp; did it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: What do you mean bad? They were not detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Right. But even though they didn't mistreat detainees, they were never beaten or killed themselves; were they?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I have just told you that I don't know whether they were beating detainees or not. I wasn't there all the time. I would stay at home for a day or two. But I personally never saw them, whether they were doing it or not. That's something I cannot tell you about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me then ask, maybe get to the point another way, sir. Were you ever threatened while you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, by Mr. Delic, as far as Esad Bubalo is concerned. He said, unless I do it I will be killed together with him, but Bubalo will be killed at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And with respect to the -- Mr. Bubalo was not a Serb detainee in the camp; was he?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, he was a member of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know, did anything physical happen to Samir Hondo or Sejo Mustafic during the time they worked in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know. I think no guard was harmed, as far as I know. Although there have been different cases, let me give you the name of the Albanian, he we called him Sok. He was detained, he was, his hands were wound with rope, he was tied to a heater, central heating. And I was sent to his girlfriend at night, I was ordered to bring him back to the camp, and I think that he was threatened to never leave number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And what Mr. Sok had done was to leave the camp; correct? Leave the camp without authorisation, he wasn't being punished for mistreating detainees; was he?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, he left the camp without authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, Dr. Gripon said yesterday that in 1992 you knew the difference between right and wrong; is that correct? In 1992, did you know the difference between right and wrong?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I believe I did, but I couldn't influence it. Nobody asked me whether something was right or wrong, if I was asked whether something is right or wrong, many of these things would never have happened. There wouldn't have been the war to start with in Bosnia-Herzegovina and all these events at Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, given that you knew the difference between right and wrong, did you ever make any attempt to report to anyone outside the camp, anyone in the TO or Bosnian Army or the police or the war presidency, or the papers, did you make any attempt to report to anybody what was going on in Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I didn't try it. And I don't believe anybody would have listened to me, because the commander of the Internal Ministry Forces who was in charge of law and order in the city would come. Had I complained to him, I would probably have not lived to this day. That was my assumption and that's what I was afraid of, and I thought it would be better for me to keep silent.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you left Celebici, nothing bad happened to you as a result of your leaving the camp; did it? You weren't physically harmed at all when you left the camp.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Maybe I was lucky to have reported to the military police. In '93, I believe, I believe, an attempt of my life was made, somebody tried to kill me when I was arrested in connection with the Bubalo case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, it's a fair statement, isn't it, that in 1992 when you were in Celebici, you liked mistreating the people and you liked killing them; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: You couldn't put it that way. I saw it all as an order that I have to execute. You know, one thing is to take pleasure over something, and another is to consider something to be your duty. If I liked it, why would I sit with the individual detainees the next day and talk to them? Why would I release, rather let Spaso Miljevic to see his mother if I liked mistreating him? I could sit together with a detainee and talk to him, but if I was given an order, I had to execute it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, you would agree that you stated to Dr. Gripon that you mistreated the prisoners for two reasons: One, that you were ordered to do so; two, that you were bored and frustrated. You would agree you stated that to Dr. Gripon; wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Could you tell me what was the interviewing question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you were here yesterday, weren't you? And Dr. Gripon stated that you told him that you mistreated the prisoners for two reasons: One. You were ordered; and two, you were bored and frustrated. He also said that you stated that you never had any difficulty doing this and that you enjoyed it. That's correct, isn't it, Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Let me explain to you. May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, maybe you can first tell me. You did say that to Dr. Gripon; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I may have said it. But that may have been in the course of my, of our first interviews. And if this is the case, then I think I need to explain this. If you go through the reports prepared by Dr. Lagazzi and other doctors you will find similar statements. That was the period immediately upon my arrival here where I was in a tough situation. In the morning I would wake up and I would hear shells falling on the prison. I would hear shots fired. For a period upon my arrival here I thought I was still in a war zone. And many things that I stated in our, my interview with the doctors at that time were not, are not true. I thought they were true at that time, and I thought I would have to state them as such. And, you know, I just couldn't get rid of all these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So what you would say, sir, is that when you talked with Dr. Gripon in 1997 or 1998, you thought you enjoyed mistreating the prisoners, but now you remember that you didn't enjoy mistreating them; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Could you please repeat this?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I understand your explanation, sir, it's that when you talked to Dr. Gripon in 1997 you thought you had enjoyed mistreating the prisoners, but now you recollect that you didn't enjoy it; is that a fair statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: That's what I stated to him at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I just asked you, sir, and you just indicated to me that what you stated to him you believed was true at the time. And so you would agree with me that in 1997 you thought you enjoyed mistreating prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: These may have been my words in the course of this interview. I said it, I can't say I didn't say it, but what I understood under those words, I cannot explain to you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. And so, you would agree with me that you were the guard who was most chosen to mistreat prisoners when the camp management, when Mr. Delic and Mr. Mucic wanted someone to mistreat the prisoners, you were usually their first choice, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: You should put this question to them why they made these orders. This is a question that I have been putting to myself time and again and I would like to have an answer to this question, why me?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, don't you believe maybe it was you because it was known that you enjoyed it and you would do it without any problem?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: No, the reason was most probably the fact that they knew that if they gave me an order, I would execute it. I would do it and not because I liked it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examinations?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now Ms. McHenry had just asked you some questions about when you left Celebici. And she said you didn't have any threats or any problems with your life then. Was there a time right after you left Celebici that Sejo Mustific came to your door?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I think he arrived the same day, in the afternoon, and insisted they should go back. He told me that Mucic, Pavo, has arranged for a passport from me and that with him I should go to Austria, unless I went back this whole ploy would fail. Then, in the course of my stay here in The Hague, in a conversation with Mr. Delic, Mr. Delic told me that Mr. Delic and Mr. Mucic had a plan to kill me and he described how they were going to do it. Whether this is true or not, I don't know. But I am just telling you what I heard from Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Ms. McHenry also asked you about detainees placed in manholes in Celebici. Were you also placed in a manhole in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection as to relevancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The conditions in the manhole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Were you also placed in a manhole in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Not in Celebici, but in Pasovici, the Village of Psasovic. In Celebici I was detained in the infirmary in Building C and this was during the winter. The detainees, however, were located there during the summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And in Pasovici, were you placed in a manhole in order to persuade you to change a statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object, I think this is beyond the scope of cross-examination and irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Moran spoke for hours about his reasons for changing his statements and changing things inside of his statements. I think this is totally absolute re-direct as a result of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ask him if he has anything to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Were you placed in a manhole in order to be persuaded to change one of your statements?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes. Together with me there were Mr. Delic, Buric Ivica and Dedic Osman. The three of us were kept there and very often. I think every other day they would come and fetch me. After midnight they would take me to the second floor of the school building. There was an office there where I was supposed to give statements, where I signed certain statements. They would even beat me up there. And later, Mr. Delic insisted from the inspectors who had done it to explain to him what they were doing and why they were doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of the usher, actually, it's in -- I'm sorry, it's Prosecution 103. If I might be handed that exhibit so that I can just take one document out of it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: I also forgot to add in connection with that, that probably also Mr. Delic and I was threatened that if we don't speak against Mr. Delalic they take us away and we'd never be seen again. And I believe that the same was said also to him. I tried to commit suicide, to jump from a second floor, but one of the investigators stopped me by stretching out a leg, tripping me, and then I was also injured slightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to show you right now what has been marked Prosecution 103. And is that a statement of a co-defendant in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how you can impeach my client or this man with my client's statement. This is just totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might respond? He started by saying Mr. Landzo was changing his statement in this Bubalo case, which he questioned from for hours earlier today. All I want to say about going into the contents of the statement, that I want to have Mr. Landzo recognise the lawyer that represented Hazim Delic at the time on this document. That's the only name I want him to recognise because it was his lawyer too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can go on. But I don't see what relevance it has to what you're doing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I would still object as to relevance because this man has told the OTP and he said, here, the man represented the 4th corps commander or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's all right. I think he wants to know the lawyer who represented him at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If you could just look, Mr. Landzo, at this statement and there is a lawyer's signature on it. What is the name of the attorney that represented Mr. Delic on that statement?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Here the name is Fjzagic, Esad, who was also defending me, but I didn't know this officially.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't need that exhibit any longer. I would like to also ask the usher's assistance to put D 80/4 in front of Mr. Landzo, please. Now at the back of D 80/4, there are some statements that you provided in 1994 to a court in Konjic. Have you found those yet?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, there are some statements here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And these are the statements that Mr. Moron kept questioning you about today? . He kept saying, you lied in those statements, didn't he say that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, the gentleman asked me about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now I would you like you to look at your first statement and tell the Court what the date is of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think the Court can read the documents themselves. I am not sure that it's very helpful to have the accused read documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I am not going to ask him to read them, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to look at that document?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, the statement was given on the 29th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And on the 29th of January, 1994, is everything that you said about Hazim Delic true in that statement?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes, that he issued the order for the killing of that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to this line of questioning. All that I was asking him whether this statement contained untruths as he told the Office of the Prosecutor. If they want to retry to Bubalo case, I would be happy to do it. But I don't think we have the time or the desire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Mr. Moran took about five hours today telling us that these things were not true. I am just going to ask him if it's true or not. And we'll just go through the piece later. I am not going to have him go through what they contain, but is it true or is it not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like a ruling on this. But also, I am going to have some, since she's opening up a fairly new area, I may have some more cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: On whether these statements are part of the present proceedings, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, those statements were admitted not for the truth of the matter asserted, but -- especially those specific statements, but solely as the basis for part of Dr. Gripon's opinion. And if you check the record, I think you'll find that I ask him if he made statements in 1994 and if those statements were untrue and if that's what he told the Office of the Prosecutor without ever going into the contents of those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think even counsel is going to read the contents of the statements. All counsel is saying that what he has stated are true to the best of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We don't even need it for the purposes of this case. It's all voracity. It will have nothing to do with this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And I would like for it to be brought to the Court's attention that the statements are part of Prosecution Exhibit 102 and they're part of Prosecution Exhibit 103 that are already introduced into evidence. I didn't know that until earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Landzo, would you look at your second statement there that you gave to the Court. And what is the date on that statement?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: The 23rd of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And, in that statement, is everything that you said regarding Hazim Delic true also?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, same objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And can you go to the next statement that you gave.

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: 1st of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And is everything regarding Hazim Delic in that statement consistent with the other two and is it true also?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: Yes. That he conveyed the order to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. I have no further questions on that line, thank you. I don't remember whether it was Mr. Moran or the Prosecutor's cross-examination, but someone asked you whether there had been a conspiracy in Konjic to prevent your witnesses from coming. Can you tell what happened to your family in January of 1998 when your money from the SDA party was cut off?

utterances.speaker: ESAD LANDZO
utterances.text: My mother asked for an explanation and the person who was issuing that money said that she will be receiving the money. I knew only after Mr. Karabdic had a talk with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Landzo, is the whole Defence of Hazim Delic based on the fact that everyone is lying, you and the Prosecution witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can't ask such a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have got a couple I would like to ask based on some of the new things that were brought up on re-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I didn't see anything new. No new material came from the re-examination. Everything arose out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you closing your Defence now?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a couple of documents that we would still like to introduce into evidence. I am not sure whether they've already been introduced. They were the medical examinations of the Prosecution witnesses that appeared in this courtroom. And we all agreed that they would be examined. And I would like to offer those into evidence if they weren't offered into evidence before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution would agree with that. They were submitted to the Court and they're Court documents. Because, in fact, the Court, I believe, for the most, requested medical examinations. But whether they're formerly exhibits in the trial, I don't know. And if they're not, the Prosecution would also request that every medical examination of a Prosecution witness be made part of the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Where a medical examination is directed at the instance of the Trial Chamber, every report arising from that normally has to be submitted to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just wasn't sure if they were admitted into evidence at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think they all have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I understand -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I understand it, they were submitted to the Court and, therefore, they have, for instance, registry numbers. They don't now have an exhibit number. And so whether or not for ease of clarity, it would be helpful to give them separate exhibit numbers, I would defer to the Court. I would think it would help clarify matters, but it's really up the Court as long as it's clear that they're evidence upon which the everyone can rely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: My memory isn't too sharp here, but which of the medical examinations are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Only the ones while the witness was here in the courtroom, we asked that he be examined by a neutral examiner here in The Hague and that's the medical report that I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just didn't know whether it was into evidence or whether I needed, you know, to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It can be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. So I also wanted to ask that with each one of the Prosecution witnesses that testified, there were photographs taken of the injuries and I believe that these photographs should also be a part of the evidence in this case. Well, there were more photographs taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I know, he himself admitted. So you don't need photographs of that. Your client himself has admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think the Mirko Babic one is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's only Mirko Babic's injuries that were admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, also Branko Gotovac, Your Honour, the hernia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We did not direct any medical examination of him. I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have a medical examination and a photograph of Branko Gotovac also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Only the Defence for the case is that is his family --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have to admit that I certainly don't want to look at it again. Anyway, is today Wednesday? I have lost track. Wednesday afternoon and the Defence of Esad Landzo rests.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just, with respect to the photos. My understanding is that the photos were already admitted into evidence and if the Defence counsel is trying to get additional photos in, we would at least be shown those photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I remember all those which you have ordered here. We have got the photos and that's nothing new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So the Defence of Landzo rests. Do you have your witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Judge Jan has not switched on his microphone and we are not getting the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I said now the Defence of Landzo rests. I would ask the Prosecution if their witness is ready. Because the other day we said we would allow that rebuttal witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes, the witness is down the block at the Promenade Hotel awaiting my telephone call. He is not present in court right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the time is almost 5.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: We'll be prepared for tomorrow morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So the Trial Chamber will now adjourn until 10.00 a.m. tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 5.25 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday the 30th day of July, at 10.00 a.m. 23 24 25
